articles.title: Priscilla Chan founded a school, 10 years later, Board voted to close it; shutdown shows what philanthropic investment means for community when it arrives, and when it leaves
articles.summary: A decade after Mark Zuckerberg’s wife Priscilla Chan launched a tuition-free private school aimed at supporting low-income children and their families,
articles.body: A decade after Mark Zuckerberg’s wife Priscilla Chan launched a tuition-free private school aimed at supporting low-income children and their families, the ambitious education project has closed, highlighting both the impact and fragility of philanthropy-backed community institutions. According to a report by the Wall Street Journal, the Primary School, co-founded by Chan and funded majorly through the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI), shut its doors un June after receiving more than $125 million in funding over roughly a decade. Located on East Palo Alto, California, the school opened in 2016 with a mission that went beyond academics. It sought to support the ‘whole child’ by offering services such as free dental care, development screenings, wellness coaching for parents and other support programmes often unavailable via traditional public schools.Why the school founded by Priscilla Chan came to a closureThe school's board voted unanimously in April 2025 to close it after the 2025-26 academic year. People familiar with the matter told the Journal the vote followed word that CZI would not fund the school beyond that year. Board president Jean-Claude Brizard, a former head of Chicago's public schools, said he gave CZI several options beforehand, including winding down. He said the board would not have voted to close without the funder's alignment. A CZI spokesperson said the decision belonged to the board and that the organization was focused on academic results rather than cost.The decision came as CZI was narrowing its focus. Staff were told early last year that funding for social advocacy had been wound down to fit the organization's identity as a science philanthropy and the current legal and policy landscape. CZI said there was no evidence that Zuckerberg and Chan's attendance at President Trump's inauguration influenced the board's vote. Brizard called the timing an "unfortunate coincidence."Academic results were mixedAcademic results were mixed. A Stanford University report found that in spring 2025, 26% of Primary School students in third grade and above exceeded literacy standards. That compared with 14% of other local students and 47% statewide. The school said its eighth-graders, many of whom had attended for a decade, reached above 50% grade-level proficiency in their final year. Outside the classroom, the school pointed to stronger results. About 85% of its students had an annual well-child visit, against 55% of Medicaid-enrolled children in the county. Three in four students spoke a language other than English at home.Former staff described growing pains, including high principal turnover and initially unclear approaches to special education and discipline. A consultant who worked with the school said new schools can take about five years to find their footing. Some features felt more like a startup than a school: teachers signed nondisclosure agreements, and some toddlers wore recording devices at home as part of a language-development program.The funding problemCZI said it had never planned to be the school's sole backer indefinitely, and had hoped the model could be sustained mainly through public investment. Chan lobbied her network for other donors, the organization said. Brizard said that was a hard sell, since donors wondered why they should fund something already supported by one of the world's wealthiest people.He also acknowledged a communication gap. The school "was never supposed to be just a philanthropic play in perpetuity," he said, adding that this may not have been articulated well enough.Impact on famaliesAbout 540 children were enrolled across two campuses. Ravenswood City Elementary School District is now preparing for an enrollment surge and is renovating a campus to avoid putting students in portable trailers.CZI pledged $50 million when the closure was announced. The money covers the remaining lease payments to the district and supports local groups carrying on some of the school's services. CZI also put $3.6 million into education savings accounts: $10,000 for each elementary student, $2,500 for preschoolers and $1,000 for children in early-childhood programs.Some parents said the news came too abruptly. Angelica Cardenas, 29, who has a daughter at the school and five relatives' children enrolled, said she learned of the closure from the news. She said families should have been told earlier. Mele Fakapelea, whose oldest daughter was in the founding class and who later enrolled four younger children, called the loss of the school's support system "crushing."Every teacher returned for the final year. School leaders helped families arrange tours of other schools, complete applications and open the savings accounts.In June, the school's only class of eighth-graders graduated. Fakapelea's 13-year-old daughter was one of two student speakers, and her family draped her in leis afterward.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 3 years after October 7 Hamas attack: A scarred Israel, a devastated Gaza and a Middle East no longer the same
articles.summary: Three years after Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the shockwaves of that day continue to shape lives, politics and security across the Middle
articles.body: Three years after Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the shockwaves of that day continue to shape lives, politics and security across the Middle East. What began as a devastating assault on southern Israel grew into a prolonged war in Gaza and then widened into a regional confrontation involving Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran and Iran-backed groups.The conflict has left behind two deeply traumatic realities - the Israeli experience of the attack, hostage-taking and continuing security fears, and the Palestinian devastation caused by the war in Gaza. Beyond the immediate human cost, the conflict has also altered alliances, weakened Iran’s regional network, changed Israel’s military calculations and disrupted diplomatic efforts across the region.For those who lived through October 7, however, the consequences are not measured only in geopolitical shifts. They remain embedded in ordinary moments, places and memories, reminders of a day that transformed the meaning of safety, freedom and home.“The smell of hell.”That is how one Israeli resident describes what a barbecue now smells like.Living close to Gaza, Deganit Bar Hay told AP the smell of burnt flesh has become a trigger, making it difficult for her to barbecue.Along the highway running parallel to the Gaza Strip, where people were gunned down while trying to flee on October 7, memorials now stand beside the road.Cars smashed and riddled with bullets have been preserved elsewhere, stacked in rusting heaps. Portraits of young female military spotters, whose warnings about a possible attack were disregarded, mark another set of lives lost that day.For those who survived the attack and those who were taken hostage, the meaning of ordinary life changed too.“Freedom has completely changed the way I see life,” Emily Damari, who was abducted wounded from her home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza and released in January 2025, told Reuters.After captivity, she said, even opening a refrigerator or drinking cold water felt like something to be grateful for. “Being free, at home, surrounded by my family and my people is something I will never take for granted again.”Eli Sharabi, taken hostage from nearby Kibbutz Be'eri, spent 491 days in captivity. His wife Lianne and daughters Noiya and Yahel were killed in the October 7 attack, while his brother Yossi was taken hostage and died in Gaza. Released in February 2025 emaciated after what he said was prolonged hunger, shackling and beatings, Sharabi told Reuters: “I choose life. I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do.”Three years later, those memories remain raw in Israel. But there is another landscape of memory just across the border.In Gaza, children are growing up with different reminders of the same war - lost parents, amputations, displacement, damaged homes and years without anything resembling a normal childhood. DW reported the stories of 15-year-old Mahmoud Abu Shadaq, recovering from injuries caused by an airstrike, and eight-year-old Layan Abed, who lost her father during the conflict.Aid groups are providing rehabilitation and mental-health support, but the scars are likely to outlast the fighting.That is the paradox at the heart of the three years since October 7.One attack produced two vastly different but deeply traumatic legacies - the Israeli trauma of the assault and hostage-taking, and the Palestinian devastation that followed Israel's military campaign in Gaza.And the consequences did not stop at Gaza's borders.What began with Hamas's assault on southern Israel became a war in Gaza, then a wider confrontation involving Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran and Iran-backed groups across the region. It has altered Israel's security doctrine, weakened Iran's regional network, unsettled Arab states, disrupted diplomacy and pushed the Middle East into a new and still uncertain balance of power.Three years on, the question is no longer simply what happened on October 7. It is what October 7 set in motion.October 7, 2023: Day the ‘iron’ wall brokeJust before 6.30am on October 7, 2023, Israel’s much-vaunted “iron wall” along Gaza began to fail. Explosives dropped by drones knocked out communication towers and remote-controlled guns, while snipers targeted sensors and cameras. Israeli defenders were left staring at blank screens as roughly 2,200 rockets rained towards southern and central Israel.Then came the breach. Hamas fighters cut through the 20-foot-high fence or blew openings into it. Motorbikes, pickup trucks and bulldozers poured through, followed by hundreds of armed men. Others arrived on motorised paragliders. About 30 breaches were eventually made, allowing an estimated 1,500 fighters into Israel, The Guardian reported.It was more than a fence being breached. It was the collapse of an assumption — that Israel’s technology, intelligence and military superiority had made a large-scale assault from Gaza almost impossible.“We have decided to put an end to all of the occupation’s crimes,” Hamas commander Mohammed Deif announced as the attack began, declaring the “al-Aqsa deluge”.Within hours, the assault had turned deadly. Fighters stormed military positions and nearby communities, reaching the Supernova music festival, where at least 260 people were killed and others taken hostage. In kibbutzim such as Be’eri, residents barricaded themselves inside reinforced rooms as gunmen moved through the communities. At Zikim, soldiers at a military base were overwhelmed before reinforcements arrived.Files, images, and data analysis are unavailable until usage resets tomorrow at 2:01 AM. Continue chatting with text only, or upgrade for more access.The scale of the failure soon became clear.Israeli intelligence had detected increased communications activity among militants in Gaza before the attack. Egyptian security services had also warned of an impending event. But Israeli officials assessed the activity as connected to a military exercise and decided that the alert level did not need to be raised, The Guardian reported. Three surveillance balloons used to monitor the border had also broken down and had not been replaced.The result was a catastrophic intelligence and preparedness failure: a border designed to keep Gaza's militants out became a route into Israel, while the forces meant to respond were caught unprepared.For people inside the communities along the border, the technological failure quickly became intensely personal.In Nirim, resident Eldad Hess and his family hid inside a reinforced shelter as gunfire erupted outside. “Ten minutes later we heard automatic rifle shots outside the house,” Hess told The Guardian. “I understood what was happening but in my heart I couldn't believe what was happening.”His family survived. Others did not.By late morning, Israel had declared war. At 10.34am, Israeli strikes began hitting Gaza. At 11.35am, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Israelis: “Citizens of Israel, we are at war. Not an operation, not a round – at war.”The language of the conflict changed almost as quickly as its geography.The attack had begun as a meticulously planned assault on southern Israel. Within hours, it had become the opening act of a war that would transform Gaza, redraw Israel's security calculations and eventually pull much of the Middle East into its orbit.Gaza became war's price, and its unfinished questionThe military campaign that followed October 7 devastated Gaza.Entire neighbourhoods were destroyed, millions were displaced and a generation of children has grown up amid death, injury and uncertainty. The humanitarian crisis became one of the defining consequences of the war.Even after a ceasefire agreement in October 2025 secured the release of the remaining hostages and hundreds of Palestinian prisoners and detainees, the larger Gaza question remained unresolved.According to Reuters, Israeli strikes have continued despite the ceasefire. Gaza's health ministry says at least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the truce, while Israel says its strikes target Hamas and accuses the group of trying to rearm and carry out attacks. Hamas denies the accusation.Meanwhile, Israel's effective control over Gaza has expanded to around two-thirds of the enclave, Reuters reported. The advance of the Israeli-controlled “yellow line” has squeezed Gaza's roughly 2 million residents into a shrinking coastal area where many live in tents or damaged buildings.The numbers tell one part of the story. The more difficult question is what happens next.Trump's plan envisaged Hamas disarming, Israeli forces gradually withdrawing, an International Stabilization Force taking over security and a new Palestinian technocratic administration governing Gaza.None of those pieces has fully fallen into place.The proposed force has a commander and commitments from several countries but has yet to be assembled. A Palestinian technocratic governing body appointed in January has yet to enter Gaza. Hamas has indicated a willingness to hand its weapons over for storage under a US-backed Palestinian administration, but Israel has rejected any withdrawal before complete disarmament.And reconstruction is barely beginning.A $2.45 billion plan announced by the Board of Peace in September is dwarfed by an EU-UN estimate of $71.4 billion needed for recovery and reconstruction over the next decade, Reuters reported.The war may have ended in parts of Gaza. The question of what Gaza becomes has not.The war crossed the fence, then crossed bordersThe first major regional spillover came from Lebanon.Hezbollah, Iran's most powerful regional ally, entered the conflict, opening another front along Israel's northern border. What had been a long-running Israel-Hezbollah confrontation now became part of the October 7 war.Then came Yemen.The Houthis attacked Israel and targeted shipping in the Red Sea, turning a conflict thousands of kilometres away into a threat to one of the world's busiest maritime corridors. US and British military action followed.Iran-backed groups in Iraq and Syria also became part of the wider confrontation.The significance was larger than the individual attacks. October 7 demonstrated that a war involving Israel and Hamas could activate an entire network of armed groups built over decades.And then the network itself began to fracture.Iran's ‘axis of resistance’ stopped looking invincibleBefore October 7, Iran's regional influence appeared formidable.Hamas governed Gaza. Hezbollah possessed a vast arsenal in Lebanon. Bashar al-Assad remained in power in Syria. The Houthis controlled large parts of Yemen and threatened shipping lanes. Behind them stood Iran, whose missiles and nuclear programme had long been central to Israeli and Western security calculations.Three years later, that picture has been transformed.Hamas lost its top leadership, including Yahya Sinwar, who was killed by Israel in October 2024. Hezbollah suffered major losses. Assad is no longer in power in Syria. Iran's own territory has come under direct Israeli and US military attack.“The old order — Iran as the region's disruptive spine, its proxies as the tools of pressure and deterrence — is gone,” Bilal Saab, a Chatham House fellow and former Pentagon official, told The Washington Post.Ali Vaez, director of the Iran Project at the International Crisis Group, put the change more starkly: “This has changed the region forever.”But a weakened Iran does not automatically mean a more stable Middle East.Shadow war finally came into openFor decades, Israel and Iran largely fought without declaring a conventional war against each other — through proxies, covert operations, assassinations, cyberattacks and strikes on Iranian-linked targets.October 7 accelerated the collapse of that distance.The confrontation increasingly moved from the shadows into direct exchanges of missiles and drones, exposing the limits of the old system of indirect deterrence.For Israel, the result has been a dramatic increase in military dominance.A former senior Israeli military official told The Washington Post that, despite the continuing trauma of October 7 and the ongoing war, Israel had reached a position few had imagined possible.“We are still traumatized from 7th October. There is still war,” the official said. “Israel is not untouchable, but we have made it very expensive to touch us.”That may be Israel's biggest strategic transformation since the attack: October 7 produced not only a determination to prevent another such assault, but a willingness to use overwhelming force far beyond its immediate borders.Israel won battlefield. What does it do with power?Military dominance brings its own dilemma.Israel's neighbours may have welcomed the weakening of Iran and its allies, but the emergence of an Israel with fewer regional constraints has also created unease.“The focus on security comforts Israelis but unnerves their neighbors,” The Washington Post reported, citing regional analysts. An Israel less constrained by powerful rivals raises questions about whether military superiority could turn into overreach, particularly in the West Bank.Saab told the paper that Gulf leaders, while wanting to see the Iranian regime weakened, also worry about “the trigger-happiness of Israel”.Inside Israel, however, the emerging philosophy is increasingly being framed as security through strength.“When this is over, I think you're going hear our leaders talk about Israel's desire for peace through strength,” an Israeli official told The Washington Post. “We are going to fight our enemies as strongly as possible and hug our friends as close as possible.”The shift is significant.For much of its history, Israel's military strength was primarily presented as a shield. After October 7, the war has pushed Israel towards using that strength to actively reshape the strategic environment around it.Whether that creates lasting security remains one of the region's biggest unanswered questions.Palestinians at centre, increasingly without controlThere is another paradox.The war has put the Palestinian question back at the centre of international diplomacy. Yet Palestinians themselves have little control over what comes next.Gaza has been devastated and its population repeatedly displaced. The future of its governance remains unsettled. In the West Bank, settlement expansion and calls for Palestinian displacement have intensified.The debate over Gaza's future has also exposed sharply different visions.Trump's plan says Gaza should be rebuilt for its people. Israeli right-wing politicians have called for “voluntary emigration”. Israel's defence ministry established an office in 2025 to oversee such departures after Trump had suggested Gazans could be permanently displaced. Trump later backed away from the idea following strong opposition from Arab states and international criticism.The competing visions leave Gaza caught between reconstruction, Israeli security demands, Hamas's future and the unresolved question of Palestinian statehood.The October 7 attack was intended by Hamas to alter the regional balance. Instead, Palestinians have emerged from the war facing a destroyed territory and an uncertain political future.Gulf states no longer just watching from sidelinesThe war has also changed the calculations of countries that were not direct combatants.Saudi Arabia had been moving towards a potentially transformative relationship with Israel before October 7. The war disrupted that trajectory and pushed the Palestinian question back into the centre of Arab diplomacy.At the same time, Gulf states have had to watch Iran's missiles and drones reach closer to their own territory.Saudi Arabia and Turkey are emerging as important players in the next regional order. Both are deepening relationships with China, maintaining channels with Russia and continuing to work with Washington — a form of strategic hedging as they assess what a more powerful Israel and a less predictable US presence mean for them.The Gulf's old calculation was relatively straightforward: American security guarantees, economic stability and the containment of regional rivalries.After October 7, none of those assumptions looks quite as secure.3 years on, Oct 7 is still reshaping mapThe most consequential change may be that the region no longer has the same centre of gravity.Before October 7, Iran's network of armed allies was at the height of its influence. Israel was powerful but largely operated within a familiar system of deterrence. Arab states were cautiously pursuing normalisation and economic integration. The Palestinian issue, while unresolved, had increasingly been pushed into the background of regional diplomacy.The attack shattered that equilibrium.Israel emerged more militarily dominant but also more isolated. Gaza emerged devastated. Iran's regional network was badly weakened, but the collapse of that network created uncertainty rather than a settled alternative. Saudi Arabia and Turkey gained greater room to manoeuvre. Gulf states became more conscious of their own vulnerability. The US remained indispensable but its regional choices became more consequential — and more controversial.The result is not necessarily a new Middle East yet.It is a Middle East in transition.“This has changed the region forever,” Vaez told The Washington Post. “But with what consequences still has to play out.”And perhaps that is the clearest measure of what three years of war have changed.For an Israeli survivor, the smell of a barbecue can still bring October 7 back.For a child in Gaza, an airstrike can mean a missing parent, an injured body or another lost home.For Iran, Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and the Gulf states, the same three years have rewritten calculations about power and security.The attack began with a breach in a border fence.Three years later, the breach has become a fault line running through the entire Middle East.From Gaza’s ruins to a global shockThe deepest consequences of October 7 are still visible in Gaza, where three years of war have transformed everyday life. Homes, neighbourhoods and essential infrastructure have been devastated, while repeated displacement has uprooted much of the territory’s roughly two million people.The destruction has extended far beyond buildings. Gaza’s economy has been pushed into collapse, with 92% of economic establishments damaged or destroyed and unemployment reaching 78%, according to UN figures cited in September. Nearly 98% of schools have been damaged or destroyed, while Gaza’s health system has been left barely functioning. For many families, access to water, electricity, shelter, healthcare and education has become a daily struggle.The war has also reshaped the geography of Gaza. Israeli military control and restrictions have pushed Palestinians into increasingly smaller areas, while the so-called Yellow Line has become a new dividing point inside the territory. The result is a population living amid destroyed homes, damaged infrastructure and limited access to basic services, even after the October 2025 ceasefire.But the economic consequences did not remain confined to Gaza or the Middle East.The war disrupted energy markets and global supply chains, with the Strait of Hormuz emerging as a critical pressure point. Around 25-30% of global oil and about 20% of liquefied natural gas pass through the waterway, exposing major energy importers in Asia and Europe to higher fuel and power costs.Shipping disruptions have increased freight and insurance costs, while interruptions to fertiliser supplies have raised concerns over food prices. The shock is particularly severe for poorer countries, where food accounts for a larger share of household spending and governments have less fiscal space to absorb higher costs.Financial markets have also felt the effects, with higher borrowing costs, tighter financial conditions and increased volatility adding to pressures on economies already carrying heavy debt burdens.The IMF has described the shock as global but uneven: energy importers are more exposed than exporters, poorer countries more than richer ones, and economies with limited reserves more than those with stronger buffers.That may be the widest legacy of October 7. The attack began in southern Israel, but its consequences have travelled through Gaza's ruins, across the region's borders and into the world's energy, food, trade and financial systems.Three years on, October 7 is no longer only a date that changed the Middle East. It has become a fault line whose economic and geopolitical aftershocks continue to reach far beyond it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: California pair charged with abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children
articles.summary: Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang were arrested at their Arcadia mansion after 21 children were removed from their custody last year.
articles.body:
A California pair has been charged with multiple counts of abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children - some as young as two months old - and dissuading a witness.

"The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented," Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J Hochman said in a statement.

Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, who US media describe as a couple, were arrested at their Arcadia mansion on Tuesday.

The pair pleaded not guilty at a Pasadena courthouse, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.

Xuan, 66, and Zhang, 39, are accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in their home to repeated physical abuse, after 21 children were removed from their custody last year.

The pair ran their own surrogacy company and are accused of making false statements to at least two women who became surrogates, indicating that Zhang was struggling to conceive, according to the criminal complaint.

As of May 2025, Zhang maintained a spreadsheet that tracked 21 children, including those born to surrogates.

Officials said the investigation began that month when Zhang brought a two-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury, telling medical staff that the baby had fallen from a bed.

The couple's lawyer Mitchell Krems said the allegation was a "mischaracterisation" based on the evidence he has reviewed, CBS News in Los Angeles reported.

Hospital staff informed law enforcement, and when police arrived at their home they discovered three different rooms called "learning centres" under the supervision of multiple nannies, which Hochman described as a "house of horrors".

The mansion allegedly had 32 motion-activated cameras which Hochman said were used by the couple to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.

Footage allegedly shows the nannies spanking, slapping or hitting the children.

One nanny, Chunmei Li, is accused of hitting the two-month-old baby who suffered the head injury two days before he was brought to the hospital.

Krems said Li was quickly fired, CBS News LA reported.

Li, 58, was previously charged with one felony count of child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death. Hochman said she was on the run with a $105,000 (£88,800) warrant for her arrest.

In July 2025, the couple's home was first raided by authorities, who took 21 children into state custody.

Arcadia Police Department said at the time the couple's house was first raided that the children ranged in age from two months to 13 years old, but most were between one and three years old.

Fifteen of the children were taken from the couple's home while six others were living elsewhere and also later taken into custody.

Krems said his client Xuan was innocent.

"He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family," CBS News quoted the lawyer as saying.

Investigators believe the surrogate mothers were from around the country and they were unaware they were carrying embryos for the couple at the same time.

Melissa Brisman, the attorney for two of the surrogates, told CBS News: "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system".

If convicted as charged, Xuan faces a possible maximum sentence of 17 years and four months in state prison, while Zhang faces up to 11 years and eight months. Li faces up to 12 years.

articles.title: Japan beer giants raided over alleged price-fixing cartel
articles.summary: Asahi, Kirin and Suntory confirmed their premises were searched by Japanese competition authorities.
articles.body:
Japanese officials have raided the country's biggest beer makers over allegations they worked together to raise the price of their beverages.

Asahi, Kirin and Suntory Spirits confirmed to the BBC their premises had been searched by the Japan Fair Trade Commission, adding that they would fully cooperate with the government authority.

There are reports Sapporo Breweries was also raided. The firm has been contacted for comment.

Asahi, Kirin and Sapporo all saw their share price fall after news of the investigation broke on Wednesday. Suntory is not publicly-listed.

According to the Japan Times, the investigation centres on the companies raising their prices in April last year and in October 2022.

All four companies announced increases, citing the rising cost of raw materials as well as other factors such as energy and transportation.

Kirin Holdings said its subsidiary, Kirin Brewery Company, was searched "on suspicion of a violation of the Antimonopoly Act".

It said it takes the matter "very seriously", adding it would "fully cooperate with the Japan Fair Trade Commission's investigation and any requests for cooperation".

Kirin Holdings said: "At present, the impact of this matter on the company's financial results has not been determined. The company will promptly disclose any material developments as they arise."

A spokesperson for Suntory confirmed "an on-site inspection" had taken place "in connection with a potential violation of Japan's Antimonopoly Act relating to domestic alcohol trade practices".

The company said: "We sincerely apologise for any concern or inconvenience this situation may cause to our customers, business partners, and other stakeholders. We will cooperate fully with the JFTC's investigation."

Asahi Breweries said it was "subject to investigation by the Japan Fair Trade Commission". It added: "We will fully cooperate with the commission."

The Japan Fair Trade Commission has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Shiranthi Rajapaksa: Sri Lanka's former first lady arrested for alleged fraud
articles.summary: The 73-year-old has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations.
articles.body:
Sri Lanka's former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations raised for a children's hospital.

Anti-corruption authorities arrested the 73-year-old wife of former President Mahinda Rajapaksa at their Colombo home on Wednesday.

They are questioning her over the 10 million rupees ($30,300; £22,800) of donations collected by the Siriliya Saviya charity, meant to be spent on a specialised scanner for Colombo's Lady Ridgeway Children's Hospital.

But officials say such a scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government.

Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing and says the money has not been appropriated.

She returned to Sri Lanka on Monday from Singapore, where she was receiving medical treatment. She had filed a court petition to try to prevent her arrest, but the hearing was set for 12 October.

Ex-President Mahinda Rajapaksa's spokesperson, Manoj Gamage, has said the money is safe in Siriliya's accounts and that no fraud has occurred.

Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president of Sri Lanka from 2005 to 2015 and for years, his family held a tight grip over the country's politics. He was hailed by many as a hero for bringing an end to nearly three decades of civil war when Tamil Tiger rebels were crushed in 2009, during his first term as president.

But in 2022, protests broke out across the country as inflation surged and Sri Lanka ran out of fuel, food and medicine.

Mahinda's brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was serving as leader at that time, was eventually toppled.

Sri Lanka's current government, under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has since revived long-stalled corruption investigations involving various members of the Rajapaksa family.

Mahinda and Shiranthi's eldest son, Namal Rajapaksa, was arrested earlier this year over allegations linked to an aircraft procurement deal made during his father's presidency. He is currently held in remand.

His brother Yoshitha was also arrested earlier this year on corruption charges.

articles.title: A Welsh man climbed Snowdon 141 times in one year dressed as Spider-Man; he raised £6,188 for children with life-threatening illnesses
articles.summary: A Welsh father turned one of Britain's most recognisable mountains into the backdrop for an extraordinary year-long fundraising challenge, climbing
articles.body: A Welsh father turned one of Britain's most recognisable mountains into the backdrop for an extraordinary year-long fundraising challenge, climbing Snowdon 141 times while dressed as Spider-Man. Dylan Hughes, from Bangor, Gwynedd, took on the challenge throughout 2025 to raise money for Hope House Tŷ Gobaith children's hospices, which support children with life-threatening conditions and their families. His unusual costume quickly became part of the challenge, attracting attention from fellow walkers and helping him spread awareness of the charity during his repeated journeys to the summit. Hughes eventually raised £6,118, according to Hope House, and presented the charity with a cheque in January 2026. The challenge also included 108 crossings of the difficult Crib Goch ridge, adding another demanding element to his year of fundraising.How Dylan Hughes began the Spider-Man challengeDylan Hughes, a father of two from Bangor, Gwynedd, had already developed a strong connection with the mountains of Eryri before beginning his fundraising challenge. In 2025, he decided to combine that interest with a year-long effort for Hope House Tŷ Gobaith, choosing Yr Wyddfa, commonly known as Snowdon, as the centre of his campaign. Hughes climbed to the summit 141 times during the year while wearing a Spider-Man costume, turning himself into a highly recognisable figure on the mountain. Hope House said the costume helped him attract the attention of fellow walkers, who would stop to take photographs and talk to him about the reason behind the challenge. Hughes used those encounters to explain the work of the children's hospice and encourage donations. The challenge continued through different seasons and weather conditions, eventually producing 141 summit ascents and a substantial fundraising total.Snow, heat and difficult mountain conditionsCompleting 141 ascents of Yr Wyddfa required Hughes to repeatedly face changing conditions throughout the year, from deep winter snow to warmer summer weather. Hope House reported that some of his winter climbs involved snow reaching up to his waist, forcing him to make his own path through sections of the mountain. During the summer, the conditions were more favourable but the mountain became busier, giving Hughes more opportunities to interact with other walkers while wearing the Spider-Man costume. His repeated journeys also meant returning to the mountain regardless of the conditions and maintaining the challenge over an entire calendar year. The unusual sight of Spider-Man climbing towards the summit became familiar to people visiting Eryri, with Hughes able to turn many of those encounters into conversations about the children and families supported by Hope House.His 100th climb became a family milestoneOne of the most significant moments came on July 19, 2025, when Hughes completed his 100th ascent of Yr Wyddfa alongside his seven-year-old son, Jac. It was Jac's first time reaching the summit, making the milestone particularly meaningful for Hughes after months of climbing the mountain as part of his fundraising effort. By that point, he had raised around £3,600 for Hope House and had also completed 69 crossings of Crib Goch. Hope House later identified the climb with his son as Hughes' fondest memory of the entire challenge. The occasion gave the year-long project a family dimension, as Hughes was able to share one of his mountain journeys with his son rather than marking the 100th summit solely as a personal endurance achievement.He crossed Crib Goch 108 timesAlongside his 141 ascents of Yr Wyddfa, Hughes completed 108 crossings of Crib Goch, the narrow and exposed ridge on the Snowdon massif. The ridge is known for its steep, rocky terrain and exposure, making it a particularly demanding part of the mountain for walkers. Hughes submitted details of his 108 crossings to Guinness World Records because he believed the achievement could qualify for a new record. When Hope House published its account of his fundraising achievement in January 2026, Guinness had not yet officially confirmed the record, meaning the 108 crossings should be regarded as an achievement submitted for consideration rather than a ratified Guinness World Record. The crossings nevertheless formed a major part of Hughes' challenge and added another physical test to a year in which he repeatedly travelled to the summit of Snowdon.£6,118 went to Hope HouseHughes ultimately raised £6,118 for Hope House Tŷ Gobaith, presenting a cheque to the charity at Tŷ Gobaith on January 16, 2026. Hope House Children's Hospices supports children with life-threatening conditions and their families across North Wales, Shropshire, Cheshire and surrounding areas, with Tŷ Gobaith serving families in North Wales. The money raised by Hughes will help the charity provide services including respite stays, which give families time away from the pressures of caring for a seriously ill child, as well as physiotherapy and activity sessions that can provide children with positive experiences and opportunities to make memories with their families. Hughes also visited Tŷ Gobaith and met children and families supported by the hospice, giving him an opportunity to see directly how the money from his mountain challenge could help.Spider-Man helped him connect with walkersThe Spider-Man costume became an important part of Hughes' fundraising strategy because it made his challenge immediately recognisable to people on the mountain. Hope House said he met walkers from different parts of the world during his climbs, with conversations often beginning because people wanted to know why a person dressed as the comic-book superhero was repeatedly climbing Snowdon. Those encounters produced a number of memorable moments during the year. Hughes recalled seeing someone climbing the mountain wearing only Speedos, while he also narrowly missed encountering former heavyweight boxing champion Tyson Fury and his family during one of his outings. His Facebook presence documenting his Eryri adventures also helped draw attention to the campaign, allowing the unusual sight of Spider-Man on the mountain to become associated with fundraising for Hope House.The challenge could return in 2027Completing the 141st climb in 2025 did not necessarily mark the end of Hughes' fundraising relationship with Snowdon or Hope House. In its January 2026 account, the charity reported that he planned to return in 2027 and repeat the challenge for the children's hospices. His 2025 effort had already transformed repeated journeys up Yr Wyddfa into a fundraising campaign that combined endurance, family memories and public awareness. From battling through waist-deep snow to completing his 100th summit with his son and crossing Crib Goch 108 times, Hughes used the mountain as a platform to raise £6,118 for children with life-threatening conditions. The Spider-Man costume made him a familiar sight to walkers, while the money ultimately went towards services intended to support children and give their families vital respite and positive experiences.You use AI every day. articles.title: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
articles.summary: The step comes after several groups complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.
articles.body:
France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials.

Several groups have complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.

The disruption continued early on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to speak about the school protests in an evening address.

Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "set alight or vandalised" to such an extent that they would be shut for several weeks, affecting 30,000 pupils.

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt.

Nuñez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions.

"There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said as he confirmed the suspension of stun grenades - weapons which are considered non-lethal and send out small rubber pellets when they detonate.

The 15-year-old boy's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near the Auguste Béhal high school in the northern city near Lille.

Authorities have said he picked up the grenade which then exploded, but students have alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired. According to the local prefect, police had been confronted by more than 200 students throwing stones and fireworks.

The national secretary of policing union UNSA said he was sceptical about the move, saying it had been based "on emotion".

"We are dealing with increasingly violent people," Jean-Paul Nascimento told FranceInfo, cautioning that without the weapon to disperse crowds there may be more clashes at close quarters. "That's where there will perhaps be even more injuries," he warned.

Concerns have also been stoked by the case of a 14-year-old hit in the face with a tear gas grenade last week. The boy's lawyer said he had lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw in the incident at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, and a police officer has been charged.

And in a separate development on Wednesday, a 16-year-old suffered a serious hand injury outside a school in Strasbourg, reportedly while handling a mortar firework.

Prosecutors also said an investigation for attempted murder had been opened after a 17-year-old student protester complained an officer "held his head underwater" while trying to arrest him near a river in the north-eastern city of Belfort. French reports say the boy has himself been charged with aggravated assault for allegedly attacking the officer.

Addressing France's National Assembly on Wednesday, both Nuñez and Education Minister Geffray said the speed at which the protests had turned violent was unprecedented.

Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France

School protests send shivers down French government's spine

Geffray said dozens of headteachers and deputies had been injured, many deliberately so, and alleged the movement had been "very quickly infiltrated by ultra-violent groups".

"We have never seen anything like this," he said of the disorder which officials report has harmed more than 200 students and 700 police officers, and prompted more than 6,600 arrests.

Nuñez later said he found it "excessive to speak of police repression of the movement", insisting that officers were only acting in response to violence and damage.

The national coordinator of the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party said that it had taken "several children being maimed for life for Nuñez to give up using grenades against high school students".

The prime minister has accused LFI of trying to "sow chaos" during the protests ahead of elections to select President Emmanuel Macron's successor in April.

Its leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently second in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally - who on Wednesday said Macron was "always on the side of attacking the police".

The president held an emergency meeting late on Tuesday with Prime Minister Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis after almost a quarter of all lycées were disrupted by the day's protests - with government figures putting the number of protesters at more than 250,000.

Lecornu announced that schools should set aside half the day for students to voice their concerns, and noted on social media that an online consultation seeking their opinions had drawn 30,000 responses within a day.

But students' unions - who put the number of protesters at 450,000 - maintain a fourth round of demonstrations is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities, and told reporters they had requested a meeting with Lecornu due to a lack of "concrete measures" outlined so far.

The union representing school leaders told FranceInfo that a solution would require "something more than simple consultation periods", while the head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, told French radio on Wednesday: "We are telling M. Nuñez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint."

articles.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to Kagan and Soai
articles.summary: The prize was given to the French and Japanese scientists for solving the mystery of life's asymmetry.
articles.body:
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.

The researchers discovered how nature exclusively makes the correct version of a molecule - rather than its mirror image.

For example, amino acid molecules, the building blocks of proteins, exist as two forms that are each other's mirror image.

But living organisms on Earth only function with one of those forms. The Nobel laureates answered the question: why does life favour just one of these mirror image molecules over the other.

In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality", so chiral molecules have both right and left-handed forms.

You can think of them as looking like our hands - not identical, but each a mirror image of the other.

And while nature almost exclusively produces the version it requires to function, chemical reactions in a lab usually create a 50-50 mix of both left- and right-handed molecules.

When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant, because each version behaves differently when it interacts with our bodies.

So, one might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing or even causes harm.

The development of the Thalidomide drug is an example of this. In the 1950s it was prescribed to pregnant women suffering with morning sickness. But it is a chiral molecule - the right-handed version is an effective treatment, but the left-hand is toxic.

The original drug given was a mixture of the two, and it was later discovered that the body will convert between the two. The result was thousands of children, born to women who took the drug, developed severe disabilities.

Speaking to the Nobel Prize press conference this morning over the phone, Kenso Soai said: "This is one of the most exciting days of my life."

By solving the mystery of chirality, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai worked out how to design chemical reactions to produce much more of the desired version of a molecule.

Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, explained: "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality - the selective production of the correct version of a molecule - can emerge spontaneously.

"The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

Henri Kagan, who is at Université Paris-Sud, first discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions in 1986. This allowed him to create a greater excess of one of the mirror images than had previously been thought possible.

Kenso Soai from Tokyo University of Science took the next step in 1995. He published a scientific paper in the journal Nature describing the first ever chemical reaction that had the potential to be homochiral - producing only the desired version of an organic molecule.

In 2003, he finally succeeded in controlling a reaction in which only one of the two possible mirror images was formed.

"Other than life itself," the Nobel Committee said in a statement, "no one had previously achieved this feat".

At the press conference on Wednesday, Kenso Soai praised the "many, many excellent researchers" in this field.

Professor Robert Mokaya, president of the UK's Royal Society of Chemistry said it was a "powerful example of how fundamental chemistry can underpin solutions to some of the biggest challenges facing society".

"Different isomers (or versions of molecules) can have completely different biological and physical effects, so they are crucial in finding effective medicines to treat all sorts of illnesses," he added.

Prof Angus Davison, from the University of Nottingham, studies the biology of chirality and said that the Nobel-winning chemistry could help reveal how and why life favours "one-handedness".

"In ways that we don't yet quite understand, the chirality of the basic building blocks of life ends up making bodies that are themselves also chiral," he told BBC News.

This was the foundation, he explained, of our hearts being on left hand side of our bodies and snail shells that coil to the right.

Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said the research awarded this year's prize has become part of "our basic understanding of how chemistry functions".

He said showing how a mirror image is created is "probably the most fundamental question in life - because somehow that happened four billion years ago when life was created. And now we have, for the first time, mimicked that in the lab".

articles.title: A UK shopper paid just £1 for a small yellow vase at a Hertfordshire charity shop; after eBay bidders raised questions, experts identified it as an imperial Qianlong piece and it sold for £484,000
articles.summary: A small yellow vase bought for just £1 at a charity shop in Hertfordshire turned out to be an imperial Chinese piece made for the Qianlong Emperor,
articles.body: A small yellow vase bought for just £1 at a charity shop in Hertfordshire turned out to be an imperial Chinese piece made for the Qianlong Emperor, eventually selling for £484,000 at auction.The unnamed shopper had no idea of the vase's importance when he spotted it in the charity shop. According to Sworders Fine Art Auctioneers, he simply bought it because he liked the look of it. Thinking it might be worth something, he later listed the vase on eBay with a low starting price.The response quickly suggested that his £1 purchase was far from ordinary. Messages and bids began pouring in, prompting the owner to remove the vase from eBay and seek professional advice. He took it to specialists at Sworders in Stansted Mountfitchet, Essex, who examined the piece and identified it as Chinese imperial porcelain.The discovery eventually led to a remarkable auction result. In November 2019, a Chinese buyer secured the vase with a hammer bid of £380,000. After additional fees were included, the total price paid reached £484,000-484,000 times what the shopper had originally paid for it.Made for the Qianlong EmperorThe vase was identified as an imperial Qianlong famille rose piece made for the Qianlong Emperor, the sixth emperor of China's Qing dynasty. Sworders said the emperor reigned from 1735 to 1796.Several features helped specialists establish the vase's significance. It carries markings indicating that it was not intended for export from China, but was instead made for one of the emperor's palaces.The vase also carries an imperial poem that "praises incense" as well as two iron-red seal marks reading "Qianlong chen han", meaning "the Qianlong Emperor's own mark". Another inscription reads "Weijing weiyi", which translates as "be precise, be undivided".Yexue Li, head of the Asian art department at Sworders, said the imperial inscription was one of the features that made the object particularly important."The vase is special because it comes with the inscription by the Qianlong Emperor, and he must have commissioned this vase," Li said.Importance of the yellow colour The vase stands about eight inches tall and has a pear-shaped design. Unlike a conventional vase meant to be viewed from every direction, it has a flat back because it was designed to be attached to a wall. Its front is decorated with floral patterns.Its yellow background also provided an important clue to its origins. According to Li, the colour had a particular connection to the emperor. "The enamel on the vase is special because it uses yangcai or foreign enamels on a yellow ground - a special colour traditionally reserved for the emperor," Li said.The quality of its production further supported the conclusion that it was an imperial object rather than an ordinary decorative vase. "It's a high quality vase because it was court commissioned, so it would have been of a high value when it was made," Li said.For the man who had paid only £1 for it, the findings came as a shock. Sworders said he had initially been completely unaware of what he had found."The gentleman vendor was in the charity shop and picked out the vase because he liked the look of it. He was unaware of his significance so he put it on eBay with a very low starting price to begin with and there was a lot of interest," Li said."He decided to take the vase off eBay and bought it in to us to take a look. He was shocked and very excited when we explained its importance," he added.£1 purchase becomes £484,000 saleThe vase was initially expected to fetch far less than its eventual selling price. According to Fox News, it had been expected to sell for about $100,000. Instead, bidding pushed its hammer price to £380,000. Once the auction fees were added, the successful Chinese buyer paid £484,000 in total."This has been the perfect auction story, a bargain find, a culturally important and beautiful work of art and a life changing sum of money for the vendor," Li said. "He is understandably ecstatic."The emperor for whom the vase was made was one of the Qing dynasty's longest-ruling monarchs. The Qianlong Emperor eventually abdicated in favour of his son, the Jiaqing Emperor. He died three years later in 1799 at the age of 87.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 3 dead, 8 injured in Seemapuri building collapse; pregnant woman, child among victims
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: At least three people, including a pregnant woman and a child, were killed and eight others, including a three-year-old child, were injured
articles.body: NEW DELHI: At least three people, including a pregnant woman and a child, were killed and eight others, including a three-year-old child, were injured after a four-storey building collapsed in northeast Delhi’s Seemapuri area on Wednesday, officials said.Eight people were rescued in an injured condition and shifted to hospitals, officials added. The body of a child aged around a year and a half, with its head severed, was also recovered from the rubble.The collapse triggered a massive search-and-rescue operation involving multiple agencies, with teams continuing to clear the debris in search of anyone who may still be trapped underneath.The Delhi Fire Services (DFS) received a call about the collapse at around 3:30 pm and rushed fire tenders to the spot. Teams from the Delhi Police, Delhi Disaster Management Authority (DDMA), National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) and Delhi Urban Shelter Improvement Board (DUSIB) also joined the rescue operation.Locals were among the first to assist in the rescue efforts. Visuals from the spot showed residents using their hands to remove bricks and rubble from the collapsed structure and helping people trapped underneath.In one video clip, a group of people could be seen pulling a woman out of the debris and carrying her away in their arms. Several people were also seen crying and appearing distressed near the site.Heavy machinery, including excavators, was later deployed to remove large piles of rubble. Paramedics and emergency personnel attended to those rescued and shifted the injured to hospitals."Eight injured people, including a child aged three years, have been rescued. The operation is ongoing and further details regarding the incident are being collected," a police officer said.The exact cause of the collapse has not yet been ascertained. However, authorities are examining whether cracks that appeared in the structure following tremors caused by an earthquake in Uttarakhand on Tuesday evening may have contributed to the incident.According to the MCD, neighbours claimed that the building developed cracks after the earthquake and that its owner was in the process of vacating it."According to statements of neighbours, the building had developed cracks due to the earthquake last night and the owner was vacating it," the civic body said.The MCD said the building was around 20-25 years old and was occupied when the incident occurred. According to local enquiries, families involved in ragpicking were present in the area, with some collecting plastic and other material when they became trapped under the debris.Police said the structure stood on a plot measuring approximately 225 square feet. The MCD, however, described it as a three-storey structure in a jhuggi-jhopri area spread over around 22 square yards in the DUSIB area near Idgah Machhli Mandi."In addition to the building, walls of an adjoining building have fallen, while the boundary wall of a nearby mosque has also collapsed due to the impact of the incident," the MCD said.The civic body said emergency teams from the DFS, Delhi Police, MCD, DDMA, NDRF and DUSIB reached the site and immediately launched rescue operations."Eight people were rescued and sent to hospitals. Joint teams of the NDRF, the MCD, the DFS, the Delhi Police and the DDMA are engaged in clearing the debris and searching the affected area," it said.There was a discrepancy in the number of people rescued in the initial statements issued by the police and the MCD.Locals said they could hear the voices of people trapped beneath the debris as the rescue operation continued.A resident of the area said several people were rescued and taken to hospitals by locals."Police came after half an hour. There is a child still trapped and some have been rescued by people and sent to hospitals. I have given CPR myself. Two to three people have been sent to hospitals," he said.The collapse comes a month after a building in southwest Delhi's Satya Niketan collapsed on September 6, leaving seven people dead and 12 injured.Meanwhile, the Delhi Traffic Police issued an advisory asking commuters to avoid the Seemapuri area as traffic movement was affected around the Seemapuri roundabout, DLF Bhopura and adjoining roads.It appealed to people not to stop, park or gather near the site, saying that keeping the lanes clear would allow ambulances and rescue vehicles to move faster.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: F-35s, F-15s, Reapers: US loses 81 aircraft as Iran war bill hits $3.3 billion
articles.summary: US military has lost or damaged at least 81 aircraft since the war with Iran began, with the value of the losses estimated at as much as $3.3 billion,
articles.body: US military has lost or damaged at least 81 aircraft since the war with Iran began, with the value of the losses estimated at as much as $3.3 billion, according to a Congressional Research Service report cited by the New York Post.The losses include some of the US Air Force’s most advanced aircraft, including an F-35A Lightning II stealth fighter and 12 F-15E Strike Eagle jets that have either been destroyed or damaged. The F-15E losses include three aircraft that were shot down in a friendly-fire incident over Kuwait on March 2. Another F-15E was reportedly shot down over Iran the following month.The F-15E, which costs more than $30 million each, was among the aircraft affected as the conflict placed US forces and their bases across the region under sustained threat. Eight other F-15Es suffered minor damage during Iranian airstrikes on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on September 9 and 10. According to the report, those damaged aircraft have since been returned to service.The largest share of the aircraft losses involves MQ-9 Reaper drones. At least 45 of the unmanned aircraft have been lost, with each estimated to be worth between $30 million and $50 million. The Reaper is used by the US military for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions as well as carrying out missile strikes.US-Iran tensions simmerThe Middle East remains tense as the fallout from the wider US-Iran conflict continues to reverberate across the region, with fresh attacks in Saudi Arabia, continued violence in Gaza and growing questions over the security of US troops.Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed they launched ballistic and cruise missiles and drones at military facilities and airports in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. articles.title: America already barred birth tourism. So what is US trying to stop now?
articles.summary: The US government is ramping up efforts to combat birth tourism, tightening visa restrictions and targeting those who facilitate the practice. Learn how these changes could affect expectant parents and foreign visitors.
articles.body: America is more than just a vacation destination for many expectant parents. Some travel to the country with the sole purpose of giving birth on American soil so their child can acquire US citizenship. But this practice has come under scrutiny in the United States, with the Trump administration taking steps to restrict birthright citizenship and curb birth tourism.In a video posted on Truth Social in May 2023, Trump said that if re-elected as president in the 2024 elections, he would sign an executive order on "day one" to curb birthright citizenship for children of parents who are illegally living in the country.During his first term, in January 2020, the Trump administration tightened the visa rules for B1 and B2 visas, saying that applications in this category may be rejected if the applicant’s main purpose for travelling to the US is to give birth. If America has already barred birth tourism, what are they trying to stop now?What is birth tourism?Birth tourism is the commercial practice in which foreign nationals come to the United States with the primary purpose of giving birth to obtain US citizenship for their child.On September 23, the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced new visa restrictions targeting foreign nationals who engage in or facilitate commercial birth tourism. It includes:Network operators: People who run birth tourism businesses and arrange travel.Visa “fixers”: Intermediaries accused of coaching applicants to commit visa fraud, helping them conceal the real purpose of their trip.Foreign medical providers: Medical professionals or providers who knowingly facilitate commercial birth tourism.Other facilitators: People who knowingly support, assist or enable commercial activity.The measure is being implemented under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows the State Department to deny visas to foreign nationals whose presence could have serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the US.Previously, on August 10, the US State Department announced that it had revoked 175,000 visas of foreign nationals who had violated visa terms, including more than 100 visas of North Africans who were alleged to be “birth tourists”.How does birthright citizenship work?The 14th Amendment to the US Constitution, passed by Congress in 1866 and ratified in 1868, states that anyone born in the United States is entitled to US citizenship, regardless of their parent’s immigration status.After returning to the White House, President Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 seeking to restrict citizenship for certain children born in the country to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present in the US.However, on June 30 this year, the Supreme Court rejected the administration’s attempt to restrict citizenship, ruling that the 14th Amendment guarantees US citizenship to children born in the United States to lawful temporary visitors and undocumented immigrants.According to the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS), around 20,000 to 25,000 mothers came to the US for birth tourism during 12 months spanning 2016 and 2017. In a separate 2019 analysis, CIS estimated that about 33,000 babies are born annually to women on tourist visas, alongside another 39,000 births to foreign students, guest workers and others on long-term temporary visas, bringing the estimated total to roughly 72,000 births a year to non-immigrants. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recorded a provisional 3.6 million births in the US in 2025.Why is the US seeking to curb birth tourism?Rubio accused “fixers” of coaching applicants to lie about the real purpose of their travel and charging hefty fees to arrange births in America.“Foreign commercial networks specialising in birth tourism have exploited the US immigration system to sell US citizenship for profit,” he said.“By restricting visa issuance of those who both engage in and profit from this fraud, we are sending a clear message: The United States will not allow foreigners to exploit our immigration system and violate the sanctity of US citizenship,” he added.Dr. Ashok Sharma, Visiting Fellow, University of New South Wales Canberra at Australian Defence Force Academy, told TOI:How will this policy impact Indians?The new restriction is likely to impact many Indians seeking temporary visits to the US.“The policy could lead to stricter scrutiny of applications where consular officers suspect birth-tourism intentions. However, it should not mean automatic denial for genuine visitors. The key issue will be whether applicants can demonstrate a legitimate temporary purpose and their intention to comply with US visa conditions,” said Sharma.The number of visitor visas issued has risen sharply from pre-COVID levels, increasing from 9.2 million in FY 2019 to 11.7 million in FY 2025.A new report released last week by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that Indians seeking visitor visas had to wait 346 days for an interview in FY 2025. According to US State Department data reviewed by the GAO, India accounted for 1,455,255 non-immigrant visa (NIV) applications in the same year.What prompted the move?The September 23 measure follows efforts to curb the misuse of birthright citizenship through birth tourism.A case that previously drew attention involved Chinese billionaire Xu Bo, who reportedly fathered more than 100 children in the US through surrogacy. A surrogate hired for the same, who identified herself as “Judy” to protect her privacy, said she saw an advertisement on Instagram offering $120,000 for surrogacy and was told the intended father was a single man seeking a large family, according to Canadian media outlet CBC News.Xu also allegedly told a judge during a hearing that he wanted to have 20 or more US-born children, particularly sons, whom he hoped would eventually take over his business. His former partner has alleged he has 300 children, while he has custody of only 12 children born in the US through surrogacy, The Wall Street Journal reported.What happens nextThe constitutional principle of birthright citizenship remains unchanged in the US. The latest policy instead targets those who help make birth tourism possible, from visa “fixers” and medical providers to businesses arranging such trips. The focus is shifting from the child born in the US to the business built around getting there.For Indians, the policy could bring greater scrutiny at the visa window, with B1/B2 applicants facing closer checks and even longer waits.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kremlin fires back after France tests nuclear-capable missile, calls strategy a ‘dead end’
articles.summary: The Kremlin on Wednesday criticised France's test launch of a nuclear-capable missile, saying Europe's defence identity was being built around
articles.body: The Kremlin on Wednesday criticised France's test launch of a nuclear-capable missile, saying Europe's defence identity was being built around confrontation with Russia and calling the strategy a "dead end".Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow viewed the launch as a "loud and clear message", while stressing that Russia remained open to dialogue.France's defence ministry said on Tuesday it had conducted the first test launch of its latest-generation M51.3 submarine-launched ballistic missile. The test was intended to demonstrate the nuclear deterrent's capabilities amid heightened tensions between Russia and the West.The M51.3 was launched off the coast of Brittany without a nuclear warhead, France's defence ministry said. The test formed part of an operation to certify the nuclear-powered submarine Le Vigilant's ability to deploy the missile following a major maintenance overhaul.The ministry said the launch was conducted "without a payload and in strict compliance with international obligations".Although France's announcement did not mention Russia, the test came after Russian president Vladimir Putin warned the West against escalating the standoff over Ukraine by threatening Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave between Poland and Lithuania.NATO has said that none of its "exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation". Putin has also said Russia has no plans to attack any European country and wants to coexist peacefully.French president Emmanuel Macron, however, described the missile test as a clear signal."Today we are stronger. The message has been sent loud and clear for wherever it must be received," Macron said in a video posted on X showing him watching the launch.Macron said in March that France would expand its nuclear arsenal and proposed closer nuclear cooperation with European partners, including joint exercises and the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory.France maintains about 290 submarine- and air-launched nuclear weapons and spends roughly €5.6 billion a year maintaining its stockpile, according to the figures cited by Reuters. Britain has 225 nuclear warheads, while Russia and the United States each have more than 5,000.The M51.3 is the latest version of France's M51 missile and entered service in October 2025 as part of the modernisation of the country's nuclear deterrent. Paris does not disclose its range, although public estimates for the M51 family put it at around 9,000 km or more.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
