articles.title: Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict: A clash of unequals, but why is Islamabad relying on air power instead of ground offensive
articles.summary: Pakistan and Afghanistan have, over the years, repeatedly exchanged fire along their international border, including in clashes since October last year.
articles.body: Pakistan and Afghanistan have, over the years, repeatedly exchanged fire along their international border, including in clashes since October last year.Pakistan has overwhelming military superiority over the Taliban regime. Yet, as in previous periods of conflict, Islamabad has stopped short of launching a full-scale ground offensive into Afghanistan. Instead, it has relied primarily on air strikes against targets inside Afghan territory.This raises a central question: why has Pakistan relied on air power rather than launching a ground offensive in Afghanistan?Pakistan and Afghanistan: Tensions despite cultural tiesThe two countries are more than immediate neighbours. They share deep ties rooted in religion, ethnicity, food and social traditions. Pakistan is also home to a large population of Afghan refugees and asylum seekers. According to the UNHCR, around 1.5 million Afghans were living in Pakistan as of early 2025, most displaced by decades of war, political instability and economic hardship.Yet these longstanding ties have not prevented repeated clashes along the Durand Line, the Pakistan-Afghanistan border that the Taliban does not recognise. The current tensions are particularly notable given that Islamabad initially reached out to the Taliban after the hardline Islamist movement once again seized power in Afghanistan, within days of US-led coalition troops completing their withdrawal in 2021 after nearly two decades in the country.The current conflict, like previous episodes of tension, centres on Islamabad’s allegation that elements hostile to Pakistan operate from Afghan territory — in this case, specifically the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). Kabul denies the allegation and has accused Pakistan of attacking Afghan civilians.On October 9, 2025, the Pakistan Air Force (PAF) struck several alleged TTP hideouts in Afghanistan, prompting a Taliban retaliation. Intermittent fighting has continued since, with Pakistan relying on air power against what it describes as TTP targets inside Afghanistan.Pakistan and Afghanistan: A clash of unequalsThe Taliban’s lack of an air force is one of the first reasons cited for Pakistan’s preference for air strikes inside Afghanistan. This gives the PAF, the world’s seventh-largest air force, the ability to hit targets inside Afghanistan and return to Pakistani airspace safely and swiftly.Yet air power is only one dimension of the stark disparity in military power between Islamabad and Kabul.According to the Global Firepower Index, Pakistan is a top-15 military power, ranking 14th among 145 countries. It also possesses nuclear weapons, making it one of only nine countries — and the only Muslim-majority state — to have nuclear bombs.Unsurprisingly, Afghanistan features among the lowest-ranked countries on the Global Firepower Index, at 121st. Taliban fighters rely largely on military equipment left behind by the departed US-led coalition forces and the former Afghan army that operated under the Washington-backed civilian governments of Hamid Karzai and, later, Ashraf Ghani. The Taliban also deploy guerrilla warfare tactics to fight their adversaries.Given this stark imbalance, air power also helps Islamabad avoid the optics of a stronger state invading or seeking to capture territory from a weaker adversary, as would be the case with a land offensive.Imposing costs, not capturing territoryThe PAF also offers Pakistan distinct operational advantages beyond the simple fact that Afghanistan lacks air power.Pakistani analysts argue that the objective is to impose significant costs on the TTP rather than capture Afghan territory. Pakistan can therefore conduct precision strikes deep inside Afghanistan without deploying ground forces, hitting individuals it describes as terrorists without taking on the far greater commitment of a ground operation.Air power also allows Islamabad to limit the scale of its operations while simultaneously signalling its intent. The PAF can carry out limited strikes against specific targets and then disengage, rather than becoming drawn into a sustained military campaign.A ground offensive, on the other hand, could risk turning the conflict into a full-scale war, with potentially far greater political and diplomatic consequences for Pakistan, including increased international pressure and the possibility of sanctions.A ‘graveyard of empires’Afghanistan is often described as a “graveyard of empires”, a relatively modern moniker referring to how major powers have failed in establishing and sustaining control over the country. Among them are the British, the Soviet Union and, more recently, the United States.That narrative is rooted partly in the geographical challenges posed by the region’s rugged and mountainous terrain. The Hindu Kush mountain range runs across much of Afghanistan, while the Safed Koh range extends along parts of its eastern border with Pakistan.According to experts, such terrain not only makes it difficult for conventional forces to move through and hold territory, but also provides favourable conditions for guerrilla warfare.Hence, this works in favour of the Taliban, which, in addition to its knowledge of local geography, has decades of experience fighting militarily superior adversaries through guerrilla and other asymmetric tactics. The group could inflict significant casualties on Pakistani troops while making it harder for Islamabad to sustain a ground offensive in unfamiliar and difficult terrain. Pakistan could therefore face a prolonged campaign against combatants well versed in hit-and-run attacks.Air power presents a fundamentally different proposition. With aerial strikes, Pakistan can hit locations inside Afghanistan without requiring large numbers of soldiers to physically enter and hold the terrain. While mountainous geography can also pose challenges for the air force, Islamabad could still avoid the far greater logistical and military burden of a ground campaign.The human and financial cost of a ground warFor Pakistan, a ground offensive would also come with significant human, financial and logistical costs. The experience of the US-led Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan illustrates how a campaign that began with overwhelming military superiority eventually evolved into a prolonged conflict. Between 2001 and 2021, the United States spent an estimated $2.26 trillion on the war in Afghanistan, according to Brown University’s Costs of War project.But the financial burden was only one part of the toll. The US lost 2,461 service members during the two-decade conflict, while thousands more were wounded. The war also required a sustained deployment of troops, extensive logistical networks and significant resources to maintain military operations thousands of kilometres from the United States.For Pakistan, with its struggling economy, the financial burden of sustaining a prolonged ground campaign would be significant. Analysts agree that neither side has the “will or capacity to engage in protracted wars.”Logistically, Pakistan, as an immediate neighbour of Afghanistan, would not face the same geographical and financial burdens as the United States. Nevertheless, a ground offensive would require Islamabad to deploy and sustain troops inside Afghan territory, protect supply lines and military positions, and potentially absorb casualties over an extended period. The longer such an operation continued, the greater the demands on Pakistan’s military and economy would become.Against these costs, air strikes offer Islamabad a way to pursue its military objectives without committing to the financial and logistical demands of a prolonged ground campaign.Air power: Pakistan’s strategic calculus?For Pakistan, the choice between air power and ground forces ultimately comes down to the nature of the response it wants to mount. Air strikes allow it to respond to developments along its Afghan border without fundamentally changing the character of the confrontation. A ground offensive, on the other hand, could trigger a major escalation, with consequences extending well beyond the battlefield.This distinction may help explain why Pakistan has so far stopped short of sending ground troops into Afghanistan.For now, therefore, Islamabad appears to be pursuing a strategy of pressure without occupation. Whether this can produce the desired changes in the behaviour of the Taliban — or even the TTP — remains an open question. But its continued preference for air strikes suggests that Pakistan sees value in keeping the confrontation limited rather than allowing it to develop into a wider war.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cornell police pressed frat members on how they knew alleged sex was 'consensual'
articles.summary: "The general rumor that was going around was that it was a consensual thing."
articles.body:
Two investigations are underway into a former Cornell University student's allegations that she was raped at a fraternity house in 2024 -- one to determine whether criminal charges should be brought and another to examine how the university handled her case.

Newly obtained videos reviewed by ABC News show members of Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity being questioned by university police in the weeks after the alleged assault.

One of the video shows Chi Phi members who were allegedly in the house that night, but not involved in the group sex, telling Cornell University police they heard it was all consensual.

One fraternity member told police in the video that "what people were saying was that there was like multiple consenting adults in this room."

Another told investigators that "the general rumor that was going around was that it was a ... consensual thing."

The investigator subsequently appeared to question how the fraternity members could possibly know the encounters were consensual.

"Dude. I was a college kid," the officer said. "I get it. I'm like, in college, I wouldn't have been like, 'Oh, that was a sick consensual act last night.'"

"I guess where -- how do they know it was consensual?" the officer questioned.

The fraternity member said he could not recall exactly what had been said but that he believed the men had told others they had sex with the woman.

"I can't recall exactly what was said, but yeah, I mean, they … they said that they had sex with her, I guess," the fraternity member said.

The officer pressed him on his inability to identify the fraternity members who were there.

"I just get worried because you know how it looks," the officer said. "You're a brother."

The fraternity member responded that he could not recall everyone who had been in the room but that he remembered Jane Doe in bed talking to people but did not recall names.

"I didn't know exactly what she was doing, no," the fraternity member said. "I can't recall exactly everyone who was in there, and like I said before, I don't want to make -- I don't want to make assumptions based on what I don't remember."

Months later, Jane Doe testified before a Cornell panel, according to a transcript of that testimony obtained by ABC News, where she was unequivocal about what happened that night.

"I was prostituted and I was held up like bait for a gaggle of men," she said. "I remember a dark room with shadows of men in and out constantly. And I remember feeling like there was a joke and I was not in on it."

She ended her testimony with a plea to Cornell, saying, "Please make it safer for those I love and the community at large ... remove those boys from campus."

Cornell later expelled two students and suspended two others but has now brought in former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent review of the university's handling of the allegations.

Yates will review how Cornell prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct, including the university's investigative and disciplinary processes, campus police response and oversight of fraternities, sororities and other student organizations.

articles.title: A couple rescued two discarded cat paintings from a skip while walking their dog and hung them at home for years; after discovering they were original Louis Wain works, the pair sold at auction for £16,000
articles.summary: What looked like two unwanted paintings in a skip turned out to be worth thousands of pounds.
articles.body: What looked like two unwanted paintings in a skip turned out to be worth thousands of pounds. A couple came across the two cat paintings while walking their dog and decided to rescue them rather than leave them behind. They took the works home, eventually gave them to their daughter-in-law and later hung them on their own walls, unaware of who had painted them. Years later, curiosity led them to investigate the pictures, and they discovered a connection to Louis Wain, the British artist renowned for his distinctive cat paintings. According to Rogers Jones Auctioneers, the paintings had been rescued from a skip and were recognised as genuine works by Wain by auctioneer and valuer Charles Hampshire.A lucky find during a dog walkThe paintings were not discovered in an antique shop or at a specialist art fair. They were sitting in a skip in Pembrokeshire. The couple spotted the two cat paintings while out walking their dog several years ago. Something about them caught their attention, so they decided to take them home. At first, there was no thought that they might be valuable. The couple reportedly thought one of the paintings could make a good gift for their daughter-in-law, who was fond of cats.The paintings were given to her and stayed in her home for about a year. She later returned them to the couple, who put them up in their own house. There they remained for several years. It was only much later that the pair began wondering about the artist behind the paintings.The Louis Wain connectionWhen the couple started researching the works, they came across the name Louis Wain. That discovery changed the story completely. Wain became famous in Britain for his unusual depictions of cats. His animals were often shown standing upright, dressed in human clothing or behaving like people. His illustrations appeared widely in newspapers, books and magazines, helping make his distinctive cat characters familiar to generations of people.The couple took their paintings to Rogers Jones Auctioneers, where their significance could be properly assessed. Charles Hampshire, an auctioneer and valuer at the firm, recognised the works as genuine paintings by Wain.Two original paintingsAccording to Rogers Jones Auctioneers, the first work was ‘Blue Cat among the Flowers’, a bodycolour painting. It was entered as Lot 43 in Rogers Jones' British & European Fine Art auction, with an estimate of £3,000 to £5,000. The second was a more unusual double-sided work titled ‘Psychedelic Cats’ & ‘Deer in an Idyllic Landscape’. It featured bodycolour and watercolour and was entered as Lot 44. Its estimate was £4,000 to £6,000. That put the combined estimate for the two paintings at between £7,000 and £11,000. But the auction results went beyond those expectations.Both paintings beat their estimatesThe works were sold at Rogers Jones' British & European Fine Art auction on May 21, 2026. ‘Blue Cat among the Flowers’ eventually sold for £6,600. The double-sided painting performed even better. ‘Psychedelic Cats’ & ‘Deer in an Idyllic Landscape’ reached £9,400. Together, the two paintings brought £16,000. The result also made them two of the auction house's notable sales for May. The double-sided Wain work ranked third among the firm's top 10 lots for the month, while ‘Blue Cat among the Flowers’ came seventh.Why Wain's cats became so famousWain's appeal came from his unusual way of portraying cats. He gave them human-like expressions, poses and personalities, turning ordinary domestic animals into characters that seemed to have their own little worlds. His work became closely associated with cats in popular British culture, and his reputation has remained strong long after his death.Interest in his life and work has also continued in recent years, including through the 2021 film The Electrical Life of Louis Wain, starring Benedict Cumberbatch and Claire Foy. That history gave the two paintings found in the skip a significance their owners could not have known when they first picked them up.A skip-side discovery worth £16,000The couple's find is a reminder of how easily valuable artwork can be overlooked. When they first saw the paintings, they were simply discarded objects sitting in a skip. They rescued them because the paintings caught their attention, not because they knew they were by a well-known artist.For years, the works remained in their home without attracting much attention. Only later did research reveal their true identity. After authentication and auction, the two paintings went from being unwanted objects to £16,000 worth of Louis Wain artwork. It was an ordinary dog walk that led to the discovery, but the couple ended up taking home two original works by one of Britain's best-known artists of cats.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kenya's first Ebola case: Ten people quarantined as screening concerns grow
articles.summary: The patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, drove to Uganda and eventually flew to Kenya.
articles.body:
Ten people who came into contact with a man who died of Ebola in Kenya have been quarantined, health officials in the East African nation say.

They are also trying to trace 57 other contacts of the Kenyan patient after he travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, dying in hospital in Nairobi on Monday.

This is the East African nation's first-ever Ebola case and there is now growing concern about the country's screening measures.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention chief has told the BBC that despite being sick for a month, the patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, driving to Uganda and eventually flying to Kenya without his sickness being detected.

"We know that he left Buta, a city in [northern] DR Congo, to drive to Kisangani. And from Kisangani, he took a flight to Beni. From Beni, he drove to Uganda. And from Uganda, he took a flight to Nairobi," Jean Kaseya told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.

"What are symptoms he was presenting? Why was he not detected?" he asked.

The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

Kaseya said the Africa CDC was investigating the case, alongside the Congolese authorities. A team from the organisation was also due to meet the Kenyan health authorities.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

Kenya's health ministry official Patrick Amoth said the patient might have passed screening after taking medications that masked his symptoms.

After arriving at the airport in Kenya's capital, he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city where he died, and was buried on Tuesday in line with health safety guidelines.

Kenyan authorities have urged people not to panic, with the health ministry assuring of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.

But Dr Dennis Miskellah, a representative from Kenya's main doctors' union, said the Ebola case did not come as a surprise to him and most health workers.

He told the BBC's Newsday programme that he had witnessed "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenyan's main airport.

"How could you have been sick for almost a month plus in DR Congo, come all the way to the country through not just any small border point, but the main entry point, the main gateway into the country and pass unnoticed?

"That's the question that most Kenyans are asking."

The health ministry says it has intensified measures to contain the spread, with a joint response involving county administrations, humanitarian partners and others.

President William Ruto has said that surveillance and rapid response teams are on the ground, building on the systems that the country adopted following the outbreak in DR Congo in May.

His spokesman said Kenya had the capacity to detect, isolate and manage suspected cases, adding that so far more than 650,000 travellers had been screened and 267 samples tested.

Facilities in four main hospitals have been designated for the management of Ebola patients, including at the Nairobi Hospital, where the first Ebola patient died.

In June, a US plan to establish an Ebola treatment facility at a military base in the central Kenyan town of Nanyuki sparked concern, with Kenyans reacting furiously about the risks of cross-border infection. The plan was halted by the courts.

On Wednesday, Health Minister Aden Duale told local television station NTV that pending the outcome of the court case, the government was considering turning the facility into the "first" infectious disease hospital in the region, to deal with outbreaks like Ebola.

More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease.

Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.

However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.

On Tuesday, Uganda's health ministry emphasised that the country remained free of Ebola and was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".

It said the Kenyan Ebola patient had transited through the country for less than 24 hours and screening teams had "observed he had a normal temperature at the time of departure".

According to Africa CDC chief, his organisation was working with all the countries in the region to reinforce response mechanisms.

Kasiye said Kenya was "well prepared" and was therefore able to immediately receive the case, "but it is not the case for all other countries".

"It means the regional approach is more important today to stop this outbreak."

However, Kasiye said there was no quick testing available at border points and the taking of temperatures was unreliable as medication is able to stop a fever.

"I have to make it clear - we don't have diagnostics to test for Ebola. It's just about temperature," he said.

Dr Miskellah, from the Kenyan doctors' union, said he was concerned that governments were counting on the "honesty and full co-operation of the travellers to self-declare, to say the truth" about their health.

This was however undermined by a lack of proper health education to destigmatise the virus, meaning people often wanted to hide their symptoms, he said.

articles.title: An Ohio neighbour removed a 15-foot white spruce while installing a new boundary fence; four years later, an appeals court upheld the finding that the cutting was reckless and fixed the damages at $11,523.87
articles.summary: A neighbour dispute in Whitehouse, Ohio, over a boundary fence and a 15-foot white spruce tree has ended with a clear message about the cost of cutting
articles.body: A neighbour dispute in Whitehouse, Ohio, over a boundary fence and a 15-foot white spruce tree has ended with a clear message about the cost of cutting down someone else’s tree without permission. The Lucas County Court of Common Pleas found that Michael Meier acted recklessly when he removed the spruce in 2022 while installing a new fence, and ordered treble damages under Ohio’s tree-injury statute. On September 18, 2026, the Sixth District Court of Appeals upheld that finding and fixed the tree-damages award at $11,523.87, according to Long v. Meier Ohio Court Appeals published on Casemine.com. Here's what happened, as per the report:A fence, a survey and a tree on the lineThe Longs and the Meiers own adjacent parcels on Neapolis Waterville Road in Whitehouse, a community southwest of Toledo. Their shared lot line runs roughly 340 feet from the road north to adjoining fields. For years, both sides relied on physical markers rather than a formal survey to understand where the boundary lay, including a wooden post in the back corner, landscaping timbers in the front yard and a satellite-dish post near the middle of the properties.Robert and Kathryn Long moved into their home in 1994 and did not obtain a survey at the time. They said a previous neighbour told them the wooden post in the northwest corner marked the property line, and Robert planted a white spruce sapling just south of that post, intending to place it on the boundary. The tree grew to about 15 or 16 feet tall and became what the Longs described as a memorial tree, with pets buried nearby.The Meiers bought the neighbouring property around 2019 or 2020. In 2022, they commissioned a survey and decided to install a split-rail and vinyl fence along the surveyed line, setting the fence about five inches inside their property. Michael Meier testified that the survey showed the spruce was entirely on his side of the line, and he removed it with a pickup truck to make room for the fence. The Longs said they had previously told him the tree was on the property line and was a memorial, but the Meiers said they did not know the tree belonged to the Longs until after it was cut down.Competing stories about use and maintenanceThe case involved more than just the tree. The Longs claimed they had used and maintained a narrow strip of land along the boundary for more than 20 years, mowing, weeding and trimming in the area between the fence line and the satellite post. They also said they regularly drove and parked along the west side of their house, using that space to unload groceries and other supplies through a side door. After the Meiers installed the fence, the Longs said they could no longer park there or open their car doors.The Meiers and some former neighbours offered a different account. They said the Meiers and their predecessors had maintained the disputed strip, mowing up to the Longs’ garden and trimming trees on their own side. They said they rarely, if ever, saw the Longs drive or park in the narrow space between the houses, and they disputed the idea that the Longs had openly and continuously used the area as their own. The previous owners also gave conflicting testimony about whether landscaping timbers and posts marked the boundary line.The trial court heard testimony from both families, former neighbours and a daughter of one of the previous owners. It weighed those accounts in deciding whether the Longs had proved adverse possession of the disputed strip and whether the Meiers had acted recklessly in removing the spruce.A trial court finds recklessness and treble damagesIn its November 2025 decision, the Lucas County Court of Common Pleas ruled in favour of the Longs on several claims. The court found that the Longs had proved every element of adverse possession by clear and convincing evidence, concluding that they had acted in a manner consistent with true ownership of the disputed strip for more than 21 years. Based on that finding, the court quieted title to the strip in favour of the Longs.On the tree claim, the court found that Michael Meier, without privilege to do so, recklessly cut down the white spruce, which it said stood on the property line between the two parcels. Under Ohio Revised Code 901.51, a person who recklessly cuts or destroys a tree on another’s land can be liable for treble damages, meaning three times the value of the tree. The court accepted the Longs’ evidence that replacing a 14- to 15-foot white spruce would cost about $3,841.29 and multiplied that amount by three, arriving at $11,523.87 in tree damages.The court also found the Meiers liable under a separate fence statute, R.C. 971.08, because they built the fence without sharing construction with the Longs and damaged the Longs’ property by removing the spruce. It awarded an additional $3,841.29 for that claim, bringing the total damages to $15,365.16. The Meiers appealed, challenging the adverse possession finding, the recklessness determination and the damages award.The appeals court reverses adverse possession but upholds tree damagesIn its September 2026 opinion, the Sixth District Court of Appeals reversed the trial court on the adverse possession claim. The appeals court said that mowing, minor landscaping and occasional parking are generally not open and notorious enough to put a true owner on notice that someone is claiming their land. It concluded that the Longs’ uses of the disputed strip were too minor to satisfy the strict elements of adverse possession under Ohio law. As a result, the Longs did not acquire title to the four-foot strip along the boundary.On the tree claim, however, the appeals court reached a different conclusion. It held that the trial court’s finding of recklessness was supported by the weight of the evidence. The opinion notes that the Longs had told Michael Meier the spruce was a memorial tree and that it was on or near the property line, yet he removed it without their permission. The court said those facts supported a finding that Meier acted with heedless indifference to the Longs’ rights, which is enough for recklessness under the tree-injury statute.The appeals court also addressed the damages calculation. It clarified that the Longs were entitled to treble damages of $11,523.87 under R.C. 901.51 for the tree itself. It then explained that the additional $3,841.29 awarded under the fence statute overlapped with the tree damages, effectively resulting in quadruple recovery for the same loss. The court modified the judgment so that the Longs receive $11,523.87 for the tree claim and do not receive a separate, duplicative award for the same tree under the fence statute.What the case says about trees and boundaries in OhioThe Long v. Meier decision highlights two important principles for neighbours in Ohio. First, courts are cautious about granting title by adverse possession and require clear, open and continuous use that would put a reasonable owner on notice. Routine mowing, light landscaping and occasional parking may not be enough to meet that high standard, especially when the true owner is also maintaining the area.Second, the case reinforces that cutting down a tree on or near a boundary without clear agreement can be expensive. Ohio’s tree-injury statute allows for treble damages when a tree is recklessly cut, and courts will look closely at what the neighbours knew and how they communicated before the tree was removed. Even if a survey suggests a tree is on one side of the line, ignoring a neighbour’s claim that the tree is shared or memorial in nature can lead to a finding of recklessness.For the Longs and Meiers, the appeals court’s decision ends a four-year legal battle with a mixed result. The Longs do not gain title to the disputed strip of land, but they do receive a significant damages award for the loss of their tree. For other homeowners, the case serves as a reminder to talk early, document boundaries carefully and think twice before removing any tree that sits near a property line.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iranian official says 'illegal routes' in Strait of Hormuz to soon be blocked
articles.summary: DUBAI, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz deemed illegal by Iran will soon be closed, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards' Commander...
articles.body:
DUBAI, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz deemed illegal by Iran will soon be closed, an ‌adviser to the Revolutionary Guards' Commander told the semi-official Fars ‌News Agency on Wednesday, referring to the southern pathway hugging Oman's coast.

Mohammadreza Naqdi said ​these "few routes" had been created by blasting and damaging some of the rocky passages in the strategic waterway and were used by "small boats smuggling oil and transferring it to tankers", challenging the narrative that Gulf ‌oil exports are regaining ⁠pre-war levels.

"The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have ⁠full control over it. This situation will continue until Iran's legitimate demands are met," he added.

A seven-day moving average for crude exports from the ​region was ​18.3 million barrels per day ​on September 30, provisional data ‌from Kpler showed, with volumes topping pre-war levels on 14 days in September.

That included Gulf oil sent via Hormuz, the Red Sea, and from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.

The IRGC has consistently denied that seaborne crude flows in the strait are ‌rebounding thanks to US Navy help, with ​another IRGC adviser Majid Mirahmadi saying on ​Thursday that a daily ​average of 10 ships transit the waterway against an ‌average of 125 before the ​war which started on ​February 28, when the US and Israel killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in a Tehran airstrike.

Despite growing oil flows ​in September, Iranian attacks ‌on tankers and logistical constraints have persisted and call into ​question whether higher flows can be sustained durably.

(Reporting by ​Dubai Newsroom; Editing by Toby Chopra)

articles.title: France suspends stun grenades after teen loses hand during student protest in Lille
articles.summary: France has suspended the use of stun grenades during student protests after a 15-year-old boy lost his hand in an incident involving the device earlier
articles.body: France has suspended the use of stun grenades during student protests after a 15-year-old boy lost his hand in an incident involving the device earlier this week.Interior minister Laurent Nuñez said he had ordered the suspension until the circumstances surrounding Monday's incident in Lens had been “clarified”. Protesters and officials have given different accounts of what happened.The decision comes as criticism grows over police tactics during demonstrations that have spread from school pupils to parents, university students and trade unions.“There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens,” Nuñez told French radio RTL. He confirmed that the use of stun grenades would be suspended “until the facts surrounding this case have been clarified”.Conflicting accounts over teenager's injuryThe 15-year-old suffered severe injuries after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade exploded near the Auguste Béhal high school in Lens, a city in northern France near Lille.Authorities said the teenager picked up the grenade before it exploded. Students, however, have alleged that a police officer fired the device directly at him.The local prefect said police had been confronted by a group of around 200 to 250 students throwing stones and fireworks when the incident occurred.The weapon is classified as non-lethal but releases small rubber pellets when it detonates.“When there is suspicion of disproportionate force, there are always judicial investigations,” Nuñez said, adding that the government was “here to protect high school students”.France's police watchdog, IGPN, has opened 18 investigations into whether officers used proportionate force during the protests.More injuries and investigations as protests continueConcerns over police conduct have also been raised after a 14-year-old boy was hit in the face by a tear gas grenade during a protest in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, last week.His lawyer said the teenager lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw. A police officer has been charged in connection with the incident.Prosecutors said on Wednesday that they had also opened an attempted murder investigation after a 17-year-old protester alleged that an officer “held his head underwater” while attempting to arrest him near a river in Belfort in north-eastern France.The protests continued on Wednesday, with more than 500 schools fully or partially closed. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu was due to address the school protests in an evening speech.Hundreds of thousands of people took part in Tuesday's demonstrations, with tear gas and water cannon used in some cities. The Interior Ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 security personnel were injured.Government faces growing pressureThe protests began in mid-September and have resulted in injuries to 215 students, 85 school staff and 715 police officers, according to figures cited by Lecornu.More than 6,500 people have been stopped or arrested since the protests began, the Interior Ministry said.President Emmanuel Macron held an emergency meeting with Lecornu and other senior ministers on Tuesday night after nearly a quarter of France's lycées were disrupted. Government figures put Tuesday's turnout at more than 250,000 protesters, while student unions estimated it at 450,000.A fourth round of protests is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities. The head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, called for restraint from police.“We are telling M. Nuñez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint,” he told French radio on Wednesday.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 3 dead in Seemapuri building collapse: Tremor claims, trapped people and a desperate rescue op; what we know
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: At least three people, including a pregnant woman and a child, were killed and eight others, including a three-year-old child, were injured
articles.body: NEW DELHI: At least three people, including a pregnant woman and a child, were killed and eight others, including a three-year-old child, were injured after a four-storey building collapsed in northeast Delhi’s Seemapuri area on Wednesday, officials said.Eight people were rescued from the debris and were shifted to hospitals, they added. The body of a child aged around one-and-a-half years, with its head severed, was recovered from the rubble, officials said.Authorities suspect that cracks that developed in the building following tremors caused by an earthquake in Uttarakhand on Tuesday evening may have contributed to the collapse. However, the exact cause of the incident is yet to be ascertained.Locals said they could hear the voices of people trapped beneath the debris as rescue operations continued.According to the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD), neighbours claimed that cracks had appeared in the structure following the earthquake and that the building owner was in the process of vacating it.Seemapuri building collapse: Latest updates* Toll rises to three including a child and a pregnant woman.* 1 child dead, 7 injured: A child was killed and eight people, including another three-year-old child, were rescued from the affected area, officials said. Rescue and relief operations are ongoing.* 4 JCBs, multiple ambulances at spot: Heavy machinery and ambulances have been deployed as teams continue to clear the rubble and search for those who may still be trapped.* Collapse at around 3.15pm: Locals said the building collapsed at around 3.15pm. The Delhi Fire Service received the distress call at around 3.30pm and rushed fire tenders to the spot.* Rescue work continues: Delhi Police, fire officials, civic teams and civil defence personnel are working at the site.What happened in Seemapuri?* The front portion of the five-storey building collapsed on a market road in New Seemapuri. The debris also partially damaged two adjoining buildings.* The building fell onto an Eidgah next to it. Locals said children regularly play in the Eidgah and the adjoining street.* Electricity in the area was cut after the building fell onto a pole and snapped wires up to the market area. Locals join rescue operation* Local residents immediately rushed to the site and began clearing bricks and rubble with their bare hands. They claimed they pulled out four people, including a child, before authorities arrived.* Videos from the spot showed residents pulling a woman from beneath the debris and carrying her away.* A local resident said injured people were also shifted to hospitals by residents."Police came after half an hour. There is a child still trapped, and some have been rescued by people and sent to hospitals. I have given CPR myself. Two to three people have been sent to hospital," he said. ‘Building expanded in phases over years’: Local residentSaalam, 42, who lives next to the collapsed building, said the structure had originally been two storeys."The 5-storeyed building had been constructed just over a year ago. It had originally been 2 storeyed. Around 2 years ago the owner demolished the second floor to build 2 more floors, making it 3 storeyed. Just over a year ago 2 more floors were constructed," he said.Locals said the collapsed building was painted and appeared better maintained than several nearby buildings that did not have plaster or paint. Who lived in the collapsed building?Kishore, 41, who runs a snacks shop next to the building, said the owners, a father and mother and their two married sons, lived on the first, second and third floors."The building housed the owners - father and mother with 2 married sons - who lived on 1st, 2nd and 3rd floor. 4th floor was rented out. Ground floor housed their scrap business," he said.Kishore added that the elder daughter-in-law had gone to her parents' house, the younger daughter-in-law was offering namaz and the father was at a godown when the building collapsed."One son and his mother were rescued from debris in a semi-conscious state. 'adh mari haalat thi unki'," he added.Most people living in the area are garbage collectors, ragpickers and scrap dealers, locals said.Nearby building had already been ordered demolishedA three-storey building next to the collapsed structure had tilted, following which its owner informed police.Authorities conducted an audit and ordered the building to be demolished.Demolition work had started two to three days before Wednesday's collapse.Did tremors cause the collapse?Locals claimed the building had developed cracks after tremors were felt across Delhi-NCR following an earthquake in Uttarakhand on Tuesday night."I was sleeping when my house shook and a thundering sound woke me up. I ran, thinking it was an earthquake and the jhuggi was collapsing because of it. Outside, a cloud of dust had blanketed the entire jhuggi. The tremors were stronger than yesterday's actual earthquake," said Sakina Jahan, 60, a local resident.Officials have not established any link between the earthquake and the collapse. The exact cause will be determined after a detailed investigation. Traffic hit around SeemapuriDelhi Traffic Police advised commuters to avoid Seemapuri Gol Chakkar, DLF Bhopura and adjoining roads.People were urged not to stop, park or gather near the site.Authorities said keeping the roads clear would allow ambulances, fire tenders, JCBs and other emergency vehicles to move freely. Collapse comes a month after Satya Niketan tragedyThe Seemapuri collapse comes a month after a building in southwest Delhi's Satya Niketan collapsed on September 6, leaving seven people dead and 12 injured.The latest incident has again raised concerns over building safety and structural vulnerabilities in the capital.(With PTI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Tropical Storm Isaias forecast to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026
articles.summary: El Niño has led to an eerily quiet season so far but the first Atlantic hurricane of the year is now set to impact the southern USA.
articles.body:
Tropical Storm Isaias has formed in the Gulf of Mexico and looks likely to strengthen into the first Atlantic hurricane of this year.

It is expected to reach hurricane strength by Thursday morning with forecasts suggesting it could then intensify to a category two storm.

It has the potential to bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge to parts of the US Gulf Coast with landfall expected on Friday or Saturday. Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches have been issued.

Isaias will bring an end to the lack of hurricanes that has led to a record-breakingly quiet Atlantic season so far with development suppressed by the growing El Niño pattern .

Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak

In its latest update, the US National Hurricane Center estimates that Tropical Storm Isaias is likely to reach hurricane strength by the start of Thursday. It will intensify further, reaching category 2 by Friday morning.

Parts of Mexico will feel the first impacts as the storm swirls out at sea, with 4in (100mm) of rain possible around the Bay of Campeche and the Yucatan Peninsula, accompanied by strong winds.

Isaias will then make landfall on the Gulf Coast - probably in Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama or Florida - late on Friday or early on Saturday.

Between 3 and 6in (75-150mm) of rain could fall across the Gulf Coast, from south-east Louisiana to north-west Florida.

A few places could see up to 10in (250mm) with possible flash flooding, especially in urban areas, and the risk of isolated river flooding.

Dangerous winds are anticipated and a storm surge could inundate low-lying coastal areas.

The US National Weather Service has issued Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches along the Gulf Coast.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has declared a state of emergency across 25 counties over concerns about potential impacts.

As the storm moves further inland and loses contact with its warm water fuel source it will weaken but it is still expected to bring some potentially disruptive wet weather for large swathes of the south-east USA as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas.

El Niño brings an eerily quiet hurricane season so far

Forecasters in the US had predicted the 2026 hurricane season would be quieter than average - and so far this has come to pass.

Isaias is the ninth tropical storm of the Atlantic season, but will be the first to become a hurricane.

The developing strong El Niño in the Pacific Ocean is responsible. It leads to more wind shear over the Caribbean and Atlantic, which can tear storms apart before they have time to develop.

This lowers the odds of hurricane formation but does not make it impossible.

Isaias has managed to form in an area with limited wind shear and very high sea temperatures - currently 30 or 31C - giving it the fuel it needs to grow.

Forecasters expect it to encounter more wind shear as it moves northwards over the next few days which should limit its intensification somewhat - but exact forecasts are likely to shift over the coming days.

articles.title: In 1974, Atlanta's Fox Theatre closed as Southern Bell planned to demolish it for a headquarters; residents raised $3 million to save it, and the landmark now hosts 250+ shows a year
articles.summary: On a busy stretch of Peachtree Street, the Fox Theatre looks less like a cinema and more like a palace that somehow landed in the middle of the city.
articles.body: On a busy stretch of Peachtree Street, the Fox Theatre looks less like a cinema and more like a palace that somehow landed in the middle of the city. Gold details, towering domes, minarets and elaborate patterns transform its interiors into an extravagant fantasy, an effect that has made the building one of Atlanta's most recognisable landmarks.According to the Fox Theatre website, the theatre opened on Christmas Day in 1929, at the height of the grand movie-palace era. Its story, however, began slightly differently. The building was originally conceived as a headquarters for Atlanta's Shriners, who envisioned an elaborate structure inspired by architectural landmarks including Spain's Alhambra and Egypt's Temple of Karnak, explains the website.The resulting design proved far more expensive than anticipated. Rather than completing the project as originally intended, the Shriners leased the building to cinema entrepreneur William Fox, whose name would ultimately become inseparable from the theatre.From Steamboat Willie to StardomThe Fox opened its doors on December 25, 1929, with Disney's Steamboat Willie among its early cinematic attractions. Its lavish surroundings quickly became part of the experience, drawing audiences not only for films but also for live entertainment, opera, dances and stage performances.The timing was challenging. The Great Depression soon placed enormous pressure on businesses across the country, and the Fox Theatre entered bankruptcy in 1932. Even after the building was auctioned, however, it continued operating and remained an important part of Atlanta's cultural life for decades, adds the report.Its fortunes changed as entertainment habits evolved. By the late 1960s, the once-glamorous movie palace had begun to suffer from neglect, reflecting the broader decline of many historic theatres as modern cinemas and changing audience preferences took hold.The threat of demolitionAccording to Atlanta History Centre, in 1974, the Fox closed its doors, and its future appeared bleak. Southern Bell planned to demolish the theatre and use the site for a new headquarters. For Atlanta, the proposed demolition represented more than the loss of an old cinema. The Fox had become woven into the city's identity, and its distinctive architecture was difficult to replace. As per the report, the residents, preservationists and local supporters organised a grassroots campaign known as Save The Fox. Instead of allowing the building to disappear, they set out to raise enough money to acquire and preserve it.Three million dollars to save a landmarkThe campaign eventually raised $3 million, largely through community contributions, adds the report by Atlanta History Centre. The money allowed the newly formed nonprofit Atlanta Landmarks to take over the theatre and begin the painstaking work of restoring it.The Fox reopened in 1975, marking a remarkable reversal of fortune. A building that had been considered a candidate for demolition was once again welcoming audiences. The rescue also demonstrated the power of local preservation efforts at a time when historic buildings across American cities were increasingly vulnerable to redevelopment.A living landmarkIt is still one of Atlanta’s most important cultural venues, operated by the nonprofit Fox Theater, Inc. It is a museum and theater with over 250 performances a year. Its programme spans Broadway productions, concerts, live entertainment and private events, bringing a steady stream of audiences through its doors.Nearly a century after its opening, the Fox represents more than the glamour of America's movie-palace era. Its survival is also a story about a city deciding that some buildings are worth saving because their value cannot be measured simply in real estate.Images Courtesy: Fox Theatre and Atlanta History CentreYou use AI every day. articles.title: A musician collected 51 rare guitars worth $1.4 million over decades, then donated them to students at Arizona State University
articles.summary: Sheldon Urlik, a collector of classical and flamenco guitars, has donated 51 instruments from his collection to Arizona State University's School of
articles.body: Sheldon Urlik, a collector of classical and flamenco guitars, has donated 51 instruments from his collection to Arizona State University's School of Music, Dance and Theatre. The gift, which ASU values at about $1.4 million, spans more than a century of guitar making, from an 1869 Francisco González to a 2015 instrument by Marshall Brune. Urlik gave the collection to ASU in 2024, and students now use the guitars for performances, study and rental, rather than seeing them kept as private possessions.A collection built over decadesUrlik is an international collector of classical and flamenco guitars who documented his holdings in A Collection of Fine Spanish Guitars from Torres to the Present, first published in 1997. A revised second edition appeared in 2016. According to ASU, luthier Richard Bruné, the collection's initial appraiser, praised Urlik for collecting flamenco guitars with the same care as classical ones. Bruné said Urlik wanted the collection to trace the evolution of the Spanish guitar from the Torres model to the international instrument now known as the classical guitar.The guitars span more than a centuryThe donated instruments run from the 1869 González to the 2015 Brune, and most of them date from before 2000. Guitars played at ASU's "Recuerdos de España" concert last fall included an 1869 Francisco González, a 1926 Antonio Emilio Pascual Viudes, a 1956 José Ramirez and a 1968 Manuel de la Chica. The collection also includes a Rafael Casana guitar made in 1910 and a Manuel Ramirez guitar from around 1910. ASU describes the collection as documenting the evolution of traditional lutherie, from early instruments built before standardised design to later guitars whose more consistent construction supports the projection sought by contemporary performers.A student found the right guitar for a competitionDavide Picci, an Italian doctoral student who came to ASU through the Fulbright Program, was preparing for an international-level competition when he arrived and needed an instrument that suited him. Martha Masters, assistant professor of guitar and president of the Guitar Foundation of America, gave him the chance to select a guitar from the collection. After working through a few instruments, he chose a 1981 Martin Fleeson. Picci said he felt a strong connection with it the first time he played it, and Masters said the instrument is making a difference in what he can express from the stage.Students can play guitars they could not affordThe collection has also reached students who could not easily buy a professional instrument. Luis Rodriguez, a Bachelor of Music student in music therapy, had been told by instructors that he had outgrown his entry-level Córdoba but could not afford an upgrade. Through the collection he rents a 1990 Thomas Humphrey guitar, which he says gives him a wider range of colour, volume and expression. Caleb Bailey and Veronica Kreeger, both second-year Doctor of Musical Arts students in guitar performance, played historic instruments from the collection at the "Recuerdos de España" concert. Kreeger performed on the 1926 Pascual Viudes. Masters said access to a truly professional-level guitar would have been out of reach for many of these students, and compared the effect to giving a computer science major a state-of-the-art computer.Urlik decided to sell, then to donateMasters has known Urlik for more than two decades through the Guitar Foundation of America. When Urlik was ready to sell his collection about six years ago, he reached out to her for help. He sold almost half of the collection independently and then chose to donate the remaining 51 guitars to ASU. Masters called the chance phone call that brought the instruments to ASU "a lightning stroke of luck for me, ASU and the musical world." Urlik said he is glad the instruments are still teaching, echoing a saying he attributed to guitarist Pepe Romero: "Every guitar is a teacher."The collection could support future musiciansUrlik also supported the possibility that some of the instruments of greater interest to collectors may eventually be sold. Any proceeds would help fund maintenance of the collection, guitar-programme scholarships and visiting artists. Audiences can hear more instruments from the collection at ASU Guitar Night on Feb. 24 at Katzin Concert Hall on the Tempe campus.A private collection became a student resourceWhat began as Urlik's personal passion is now an educational resource for a new generation of players. The 51 guitars preserve instruments from different eras while letting students play them rather than view them behind glass. For students such as Picci and Rodriguez, the collection provides professional-level instruments at a formative point in their careers.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Kemi Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes
articles.summary: Tory leader says her party is "coming back", as she aims to convince voters it has changed after 2024 election defeat.
articles.body:
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has pledged to scrap inheritance tax (IHT) on family homes while also allowing couples to leave £1m tax-free, in her keynote speech at the party's conference in Birmingham.

Badenoch added her ambition would be for a Conservative government to abolish IHT "as soon as we can afford it", but said she could not currently propose this due to spending commitments on defence, prisons and the economy.

Badenoch also used her speech to try to make clear how the Tories differed to Labour and Reform UK.

She pitched them as the "no-nonsense party" compared to the Reform UK "circus" and accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to "live in the past".

Tories united behind Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters

Why Tories are talking about winning the next election

What's in the Conservatives' inheritance tax plan and who benefits?

Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for wealthier people in the country.

Badenoch arrived in Birmingham's Symphony Hall with a message to Conservative Party members that they face a "battle for the soul of the this nation".

She argued her party is "renewed" and "coming back" as she continued efforts to convince voters that it has changed following an historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

In a nod to those who have defected to Nigel Farage's party, Badenoch said: "The Conservatives have had an export boom of drama queens going to Reform.

"This party is now the no drama party, we are the no-nonsense party."

With the party trailing Labour and Reform in the polls, Badenoch acknowledged that people are "looking through the shop window", they "like what they see" but "not enough of them are buying yet, we need to fix that".

Her inspiration for how to revive a long-standing brand was Marks and Spencer (M&S), saying they have "adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back".

Badenoch added: "Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust and make people feel good about our party again."

One of the biggest responses in the room from members came as Badenoch made clear she did not want to do an election deal with Reform.

She described many Reform voters as "our people", adding: "We let them down and we want them to come back home."

Following a section of the speech mocking some of Reform's senior figures, Badenoch said: "To those who say 'unite the right', we are not uniting with that.

"People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that. Character, conduct, and standards matter."

She also said she did not want to live in a country run by people who "debate whether my mixed-race children are English".

In one of many jibes aimed at Burnham, Badenoch labelled him a "Paddington Bear prime minister" who was "hoping that the problems will just go away".

In the days ahead of Wednesday's speech, there was widespread speculation that Badenoch would announce changes to IHT.

As the opposition leader neared the end of her 66-minute speech, she said IHT was "supposed to be a tax on the super wealthy" but it is "now a tax on ordinary middle-class families in every corner of our country".

She said: "The next Conservative government will legislate so nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home.

"On top of that, couples would be able to leave an additional £1m tax-free and these changes mean every inheritance tax bill will be cut and the number of families paying inheritance tax will fall by more than half."

The Conservatives have estimated the policy would cost around £6bn a year and believe they have identified £71bn of savings that can be made to government spending, including welfare cuts.

Under the current rules, estates worth more than £325,000, or £500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren, can face a 40% tax rate on assets above the threshold.

Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other.

In 2023-24, 4.72% of UK deaths resulted in an IHT charge and raised around £7bn for the government.

Badenoch also said her "ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it".

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories haven't changed.

"Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories' choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead."

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said Badenoch had "chickened out of doing anything big" and is "for the 2%".

The former Tory MP said: "While the Tory Party is offering handouts to multi-millionaires, Reform will give everyone a £500 tax cut by raising the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.

"The Tory Party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country."

Elsewhere in her speech, Badenoch referred to other policies the party has announced in recent days.

These include a £10bn anti-missile defence system , 50,000 new prison places and halving the rate of employer national insurance on earnings for people aged between 21 to 24.

They also pledged to scrap the "cliff edge" that means parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.

Another policy to be scrapped would be the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), dubbed the "mansion tax".

This is due to take effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m.

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey responded to the speech by saying Badenoch had been "lecturing the country on fiscal responsibility while making tens of billions in unfunded promises".

Green MP Carla Denyer added: "Kemi Badenoch once again defined the Conservative Party as pro-billionaires, pro-inequality and pro-damaging the environment."

articles.title: BJD joins INDIA bloc's SIR protest, to stay away from Odisha bandh: Naveen Patnaik plays the balancing act, again
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Is Naveen Patnaik’s Biju Janata Dal (BJD) cosying up to the opposition’s INDIA bloc?
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Is Naveen Patnaik’s Biju Janata Dal (BJD) cosying up to the opposition’s INDIA bloc? On Tuesday, the BJD joined the opposition coalition’s protest march against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in the national capital. The BJD leaders, however, were quick to clarify that their participation in the protest did not mean the BJD was joining the opposition coalition.Senior BJD leader and chief whip in Odisha assembly Pramila Mallik explained the party’s support for the protest march and said, “Naveen Patnaik noticed that the CEC had committed irregularities in the SIR process and EVMs and felt that action should be taken against Gyanesh Kumar for misleading the voters and youth of India and mismanaging the voter list. Since the INDIA bloc’s rally was organised against the CEC, the BJD MPs joined the march.”BJD parliamentary party leader in Rajya Sabha Manas Mangaraj, who joined the opposition protest march, had echoed similar stand on Tuesday. "The BJD has maintained equal distance from both the INDIA bloc and the NDA. However, as a responsible political party committed to protecting democratic institutions and the integrity of the electoral process, the BJD will participate in today’s programme as directed by our leader Naveen Patnaik," he had said before joining the protest.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Mallik also clarified that neither the regional party nor its MPs, who joined the protest march, had joined any political group, and that the party still adhered to its equidistance policy.Interestingly, Mallik, who had earlier announced that the BJD will support INDIA bloc’s Odisha bandh call on October 8, clarified that her party will not participate in the opposition bloc’s agitation in the state. “The BJD is not part of any particular bloc and will not support any programme by any group,” the BJD leader said. She also clarified that the INDIA bloc had not held any discussions with the BJD.The 12-hour bandh, called by nine parties of the INDIA bloc for Thursday, is also demanding the resignation of Odisha school and mass education minister Nityananda Gond over alleged errors in school textbooks.Decoding BJD's middle pathSenior journalist and political analyst Jatindra Dash feels the BJD is indulging in political posturing to strike a balance.“They are trying to demonstrate that they are maintaining an equal distance from both the blocs. They don’t want to appear hostile to either of the two coalitions. But then, they also don’t want to give the Congress in the state an opportunity to say that BJD did not oppose the BJP on allegations of vote chori. That explains why they joined the Delhi protest but will keep away from the agitation in the state,” Jatindra Dash says.“The BJD will play the wait-and-watch game. If at any stage they see the BJP weakening, they will come out openly against the saffron party and, if needed, even associate with the INDIA bloc. But it is unlikely that any such thing will happen in the near future,” he adds.“The BJD still has a strong organisation, and if there is anti-incumbency against the BJP government in Odisha, Naveen Patnaik will gain as the Congress in the state is nowhere in the picture as of now,” Jatindra Dash says.That perhaps explains why the BJD is still walking the middle path in politics.The BJD has long maintained a neutral political stand by staying equidistant from both the BJP-led NDA and the Congress-led INDIA bloc. However, on several occasions in the past, Naveen Patnaik’s party has bailed out the Narendra Modi-led NDA government on key legislations in Parliament.Some of the initiatives of the Modi government since 2014 that got BJD’s backing include:Demonetisation Bill Goods and Services Tax (GST)Triple Talaq Bill Dilution of Article 370 The Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA)When faced with criticism from the opposition parties for helping the BJP, the BJD cited national interest to justify support to these Central legislations. Jatindra Dash says BJD has always chosen the politics of non-confrontation and balance while strongly safeguarding its regional identity.“BJD is a regional party and they appear to have some compulsions. They don't want to be seen as confrontational with the party that is in power at the Centre. Also, initially the BJD leadership’s assumption would have been that the BJP may renew its coalition with the party. That perhaps explains why the BJD backed several key legislations of the Modi government,” Jatindra says to explain Naveen Patnaik’s support to the NDA.Can BJD bounce back?However, the BJD paid a heavy political price for this support as the BJP decimated Naveen Patnaik’s party in the 2024 elections - both in the Lok Sabha and the assembly elections.In the 2024 assembly election, the BJP won 78 of the 147 seats in Odisha assembly, while the BJD got 51, the Congress 14, the Communist Party of India (Marxist) 1, and Independents 3. In the Lok Sabha election, the saffron party won 20 of the 21 seats in Odisha, while the Congress took 1.BJD leaders have cited the party’s vote share of 40.22 per cent in the assembly elections against the BJP’s 40.07 per cent to claim that Naveen Patnaik’s popularity remains intact and the party will bounce back.However, the fact remains that in the last two years, BJD has lost several of its prominent leaders and MPs to the BJP. In what can be described as a late rearguard action, Naveen Patnaik in June this year convened a meeting of party leaders who unsuccessfully contested the 2024 Odisha assembly elections.The meeting lasted nearly three hours and saw the BJD supremo interact directly with more than 70 leaders, listening to their feedback, concerns and suggestions regarding the party’s future course of action.The road ahead for the BJD in Odisha remains full of challenges. Naveen Patnaik won five consecutive elections, ruled the state for 24 long years before the BJP ended his winning streak. He still enjoys popularity in the state and has control over the organization. For Naveen Patnaik and his BJD the challenge would be to ensure that they don’t lose relevance and instead function as a strong opposition, not ceding any space to the Congress.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: David Attenborough's Blue Planet III uncovers 'surprising and intelligent' sea creatures
articles.summary: Sir David says the series uncovers marine life that is "even more precious than we ever realised".
articles.body:
Sir David Attenborough has promised to "venture even further" and uncover marine life that is "more precious than we ever realised" in Blue Planet III.

The broadcaster, who turned 100 earlier this year , narrates the new six-part series exploring the darkest depths of the world's oceans, produced by the BBC Natural History Unit in Bristol.

After almost four years of filming, the latest instalment in the franchise will air on the BBC later this autumn, marking 25 years since the first series premiered.

At a launch event on Tuesday, Sir David said: "When I narrated the first Blue Planet series, it didn't occur to me that I would be narrating a third series in my centennial year."

Two-year revamp of suspension bridge is complete

'Joy and inclusion' at black trail running event

New red route could be introduced in parts of Bristol

The production uses advanced equipment including remote underwater cameras, drones, and manned submersibles to capture newly discovered animal behaviours.

Viewers are taken into some of the world's least understood marine environments, ranging from coral reefs and tropical islands to the darkest depths of the ocean.

In the newly released extended trailer, Attenborough promised to "venture even further" than ever before, describing the ocean as "an endlessly fascinating place".

"We will uncover life that is more surprising, more intelligent, and even more precious than we ever realised," he said.

"We will discover the extraordinary relationship we have with the ocean. One that has never been more important to understand."

Sir David said he was "proud and delighted" to be associated with the project.

The new series is accompanied by an original score from Hans Zimmer and Bleeding Fingers Music.

Zimmer, who also scored Blue Planet II, said the series was the "most important work" he has ever done.

"I think everybody who comes to Blue Planet comes to it with the knowledge that it is something that changes the world by making you fall in love," he said.

"It's not something where you're being lectured or cajoled about things, but it's something that just shows you how spectacular and beautiful our world truly is.

"How we need to preserve it and how we need to love it, and how whatever we love, we need to treat with great kindness and great respect."

It also features an original song, Into The Deep (Seas Cry) co-written by Jade Thirlwall - best known for being a member of the pop group Little Mix.

Thirlwall described herself as a "huge fan" of the franchise, praising Attenborough as "a true hero".

"Being part of Blue Planet III in this way feels incredibly special and a real privilege," she added.

The premiere launch event took place at Piccadilly Circus in London on Tuesday, with footage from the new series taking over the digital displays.

articles.title: In 2014, Massachusetts built State Route 7A’s rail overpass with stacked soil-and-fabric walls, cutting the $1.1 million project cost by 49%
articles.summary: In 2014, Massachusetts revolutionized bridge construction by using Geosynthetic Reinforced Soil-Integrated Bridge Systems (GRS-IBS) for the State Route 7A project, resulting in a 49% cost reduction. This innovative approach minimized disruption, accommodated a skewed bridge over an active railroad, and showcased effective monitoring methods post-construction.
articles.body: Massachusetts replaced the State Route 7A bridge over the Housatonic Railroad in Sheffield in 2014 by making use of a construction system that replaced conventional bridge abutments. They achieved this with layers of compacted soil and synthetic reinforcement, and called it GRS-IBS, which was the state's first project using the technology.The $1.1 million bridge cost 49% less than the estimated price of the original conventional design, according to the Federal Highway Administration. The project also had to accommodate a railway crossing that required a 105-foot-wide bridge with a 30-degree skew.The bridge used layers instead of a conventional abutmentThe geosynthetic reinforced soil portion uses alternating layers of compacted granular fill and sheets of geosynthetic reinforcement. The integrated bridge system places a bridge superstructure directly on those reinforced soil abutments, which creates a continuous transition between the road and the bridge. FHWA had been promoting GRS-IBS through its Every Day Counts program in order to build smaller bridges more quickly and at lower cost. FHWA says the technology can reduce construction costs because the abutments use readily available fill material and reinforcement instead of some of the heavier conventional concrete construction.The Route 7A project presented a more demanding application, since the bridge had to cross an active railroad and was built with a 30-degree skew. FHWA later identified it as one of the larger GRS-IBS structures that was constructed at the time, with abutments roughly 24 and 28 feet high. FHWA reported that the 2014 project was built with minimal disruption to train traffic, and the completed structure provided the wider roadway and pedestrian facilities that were required for the replacement while using the reinforced-soil system underneath.Engineers watched the walls after constructionA later FHWA synthesis report says that the Route 7A bridge included survey targets on the wall faces, inclinometers to measure lateral movement within the abutments, and earth-pressure cells beneath and behind the bridge girders. The monitoring was done with the intention of tracking how the reinforced soil structure behaved after construction.The report recorded less than 2 inches of settlement in the GRS-IBS structure, and lateral movement remained within a range of about 0.2 inches and appeared to vary with temperature. The data were part of a larger effort to evaluate GRS-IBS structures and determine where the system could be used on future bridge projects.A bridge that crosses a railway at an angle can create different loading and movement conditions from a straightforward perpendicular crossing, and FHWA and the Massachusetts Department of Transportation therefore continued to monitor the structure after it opened. The project was also part of a broader push by transportation agencies to shorten bridge construction and reduce costs, with the GRS-IBS construction using compacted soil and reinforcement for the abutment walls, while the bridge deck itself can use conventional structural components.A large saving on a relatively small bridgeFHWA reported that the $1.1 million GRS-IBS bridge represented a 49% saving in comparison with the estimated cost of the original conventional design. The system changed how the bridge approaches and abutments were constructed, and FHWA describes GRS-IBS as a method that combines reinforced soil with the bridge superstructure rather than treating the roadway and bridge as entirely separate conventional components.In June 2014, MassDOT and FHWA held a workshop in Massachusetts that was focused on GRS-IBS. The Route 7A project in Sheffield was presented as the state's first example, while two additional Massachusetts projects were already being developed. The Route 7A bridge therefore served two purposes: replacing an aging railway crossing and giving Massachusetts engineers a full-scale example of how reinforced soil could be used for a skewed bridge over an active rail line. Its construction changed the structure supporting conventional bridge components, and the cost comparison of a $1.1 million project coming in 49% below the estimated conventional design was the clearest result.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘TV drama cannot alter reality': India slams Pakistan over cross-border terror
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India has fiercely condemned Pakistan for continuing to sponsor cross-border terrorism, declaring that televised media campaigns cannot alter
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India has fiercely condemned Pakistan for continuing to sponsor cross-border terrorism, declaring that televised media campaigns cannot alter the grim facts on the ground.Ministry of external affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal delivered the scathing rebuke during a press briefing in New Delhi on Wednesday. The statement follows a series of intense diplomatic clashes at the 81st United Nations general assembly (UNGA) and ongoing regional tensions."Pakistan is a country which has been fueling cross-border terrorism for years; lying and propagating falsehoods have become second nature to it," Jaiswal told reporters.New Delhi’s latest offensive targets what it calls Pakistan's ongoing public relations campaigns and media narratives. The MEA dismissed these broadcasts as an attempt to deflect international accountability and project a false image of peace."I want to emphasise that no matter how hard they try, the drama staged for television cannot alter the ground reality," Jaiswal added.The diplomatic row has escalated rapidly following sharp exchanges at the UNGA in New York. India recently exercised its Right of Reply at the UN to counter Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Indian diplomats strongly rejected Sharif's statements, accusing Islamabad of using falsehoods and deceit to mislead the global community.Bilateral relations have remained severely strained since India launched Operation Sindoor. The retaliatory precision airstrikes targeted terrorist infrastructure across the Line of Control.With this latest statement, India has reaffirmed its rigid stance on regional security. New Delhi maintains that normal diplomatic engagement is impossible until Islamabad takes verifiable action to dismantle terror launchpads on its soil.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
