articles.title: Rolling Stones bassist Bill Wyman took up metal detecting after workers found a medieval jug at his Suffolk home; his searches later uncovered more than 200 Roman coins and a previously unknown farmstead
articles.summary: Bill Wyman, best known as the original bassist of the Rolling Stones, turned an accidental discovery on his Suffolk property into a serious pursuit of
articles.body: Bill Wyman, best known as the original bassist of the Rolling Stones, turned an accidental discovery on his Suffolk property into a serious pursuit of archaeology. After workers digging at his country home unearthed a medieval jug, he took up metal detecting to explore the land further. Over time, his searches revealed more than 200 Roman coins and the remains of a previously unknown Roman farmstead, findings that were recorded with the Suffolk Heritage Explorer and documented on his own archaeology pages. Read on to know more about it here:From a medieval jug to a new hobbyThe story began not with a grand plan but with routine work on Wyman’s estate in Suffolk, in eastern England.Workers excavating on the property came across a medieval jug, an object that immediately suggested the land had been used and inhabited long before modern times. That single find sparked Wyman’s curiosity about what else might lie beneath the surface.Rather than simply pocketing the jug and moving on, Wyman decided to investigate more systematically. He took up metal detecting, a hobby that is popular in the UK but also tightly regulated, especially on land with known or suspected archaeological significance. His approach was not that of a casual treasure hunter but of someone willing to learn the rules, record finds properly and work with heritage authorities.That decision set the stage for a series of discoveries that would go far beyond a single stray artefact.What began as an answer to one medieval object became a lifelong passion for the history of his country and the wider region. Metal detecting was Wyman’s way of engaging with the past in a practical way, as well as his long-standing interest in history and heritage.More than 200 Roman coins emergeAs Wyman scanned the fields around his Suffolk home, his detector began to pick up signals that pointed to a much older layer of history. Over multiple sessions, he recovered more than 200 Roman coins from the property.These coins mark different periods of Roman occupation in Britain, a tangible link to the centuries when the region was part of the Roman Empire. Roman coin hoards and scattered finds are common in eastern England, where Roman settlements, roads and farms were once widespread. But the concentration of coins on Wyman’s land pointed to this not being just a matter of a few lost coins.The number and distribution of the coins suggested ongoing activity in the region, perhaps linked to a larger settlement or working farm. Details of each coin were recorded, including its position, condition and approximate date. In the UK, finds like these are generally reported through the Portable Antiquities Scheme, which helps museums and archeologists keep track of finds and build up a picture of past human activity. Wyman’s adherence to these procedures meant the coins could contribute to scholarly knowledge rather than vanish into private collections.Uncovering a lost Roman farmsteadThe coins were only part of the story. As Wyman continued to search and record his finds, patterns began to emerge that pointed to something more substantial than scattered losses. The distribution of artefacts, combined with surface features and local topography, suggested the presence of a Roman farmstead that had not been previously identified in official records.That site was eventually entered into the Suffolk Heritage Explorer, the county’s historic environment record, under the monument number MSF6324. The entry describes a Roman farmstead located within the parish where Wyman’s property lies, noting the metal-detected finds that helped define its extent.By being recorded in this way, the site became part of the public archaeological record, available to researchers and planners who need to consider heritage when making decisions about land use.A Roman farmstead would have included buildings such as barns, workshops and living quarters, along with fields, trackways and possibly enclosures for animals. Over time, the wooden and stone structures decayed or were robbed out, leaving behind traces in the soil, scattered pottery, metalwork and coins. Metal detecting can help map those traces, especially when combined with careful recording and, where appropriate, limited excavation.A disciplined approach to detectingWyman’s work on his Suffolk land reflects a broader shift in how metal detecting is viewed in the UK.Once sometimes seen as a threat to archaeology, responsible detecting is now recognised as a valuable source of information when practitioners follow the code of practice, report finds and work with landowners and heritage bodies. Wyman’s own website emphasises his commitment to responsible archaeology and to recording finds properly.That discipline matters because context is everything in archaeology. A coin on its own tells part of a story, but its location, depth and relationship to other finds can reveal much more about how people lived, worked and moved across the landscape. By keeping detailed records and sharing them with Suffolk’s heritage team, Wyman helped turn personal discoveries into data that can be used by specialists.His approach also points to the importance of landowners.As the owner of the property, Wyman could authorize systematic digging, ensure finds were recorded and prevent others from digging without reporting their discoveries. This type of control is essential for protecting archeological sites from looting or unscientific removal of artifacts, which can obliterate valuable information. Rock star to recorded discoverer For the general public, Bill Wyman is often linked with the Rolling Stones, their concerts, records and cultural influence. His archeological work presents another side to his life, one of quiet fields, meticulous recording and the gradual accumulation of evidence about the past.On his website, he presents his archaeology as a serious interest, with pages devoted to finds, methods and the importance of preserving heritage.The Roman farmstead and coin finds in Suffolk add to a wider pattern of Wyman’s engagement with history. He has long been interested in historical subjects, from early rock and roll to older periods of British and European history. Archaeology allows him to participate directly in uncovering that past, rather than simply reading about it or collecting objects second-hand.At the same time, his profile helps draw attention to the value of responsible metal detecting and the role of private landowners in protecting archaeological sites.When high-profile figures follow the rules and work with heritage authorities, it sets an example for others who might be tempted to treat detecting as a purely commercial activity.A site that now belongs to the recordThe Roman farmstead recorded as MSF6324 is no longer just a private curiosity on Wyman’s land. It is part of Suffolk’s historic environment record, referenced in planning, research and conservation work. Anyone studying Roman settlement in the area, or assessing the impact of proposed developments nearby, will now encounter this site as part of the known archaeological landscape.That transition from private discovery to public record is one of the most important outcomes of Wyman’s work. The coins and other finds could have remained a personal collection, interesting but largely invisible to scholars. Instead, they have been integrated into the county’s understanding of its past, helping to fill gaps in the map of Roman activity in Suffolk.For Wyman, the project shows how a single medieval jug can open a door to a much deeper history. What began as a chance find during routine work grew into a sustained investigation that revealed a lost farmstead and hundreds of coins.In doing so, it turned a piece of private land into a small but meaningful chapter in the story of Roman Britain.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'We want you home’: Family of missing UMD student Dilan Ashar appeals for help as search enters 5th day
articles.summary: The family of 22-year-old University of Maryland student Dilan Shaan Ashar has made an emotional appeal for help as authorities continue searching for
articles.body: The family of 22-year-old University of Maryland student Dilan Shaan Ashar has made an emotional appeal for help as authorities continue searching for him, days after he disappeared from the university campus. "Dilan, we love you so much and we hope you are safe. We want you home," said his mother in the recorded video message released through the University of Maryland Police Department, urging students and members of the community to share his photographs and look for any information that could help locate him.Ashar was last seen on surveillance footage at around 2:30 am on October 2 at the Terrapin Trail Garage on the University of Maryland’s College Park campus. Police said he had left his residence at about 2 am that morning.His parents last communicated with him at around 6 pm on October 1. They became concerned after they went to his residence the following day and found that he was not there.Police have described Ashar as 6 feet 2 inches tall and weighing about 185 pounds. At the time he was last seen, he was wearing a black University of Maryland hooded sweatshirt, grey sweatpants and white shoes.His family said he does not have his cellphone, wallet or identification with himNo sign of Ashar even after drone searcg, K-9 searchAuthorities have carried out multiple searches since Ashar was reported missing.On October 3, police used a drone to search wooded areas near the Terrapin Trail Garage and later conducted a K-9 search. The following morning, nearly 50 first responders and nine dogs searched approximately 110 acres around the garage. Police also used a drone to search the university golf course.Officers have repeatedly checked parking garages, wooded areas, Lake Artemesia and nearby parks. However, all searches conducted so far have failed to locate Ashar.Police are continuing to review surveillance footage and have released images showing Ashar outside the Terrapin Trail Garage in the early hours of October 2.Family asks public to check camerasAshar’s family and police are asking people who live or work near the university to check security-camera footage from their homes, vehicles and businesses for anything that could help investigators establish where he went.Police are also urging people to share Ashar’s photographs and missing-person information on social media.Anyone who may have information about Ashar’s whereabouts has been asked to contact the University of Maryland Police Department at 301-405-3555. Anonymous tips can also be submitted through the department’s website.The case has been classified as a critical missing-person investigation. Police said they will continue searching for Ashar and rechecking previously searched areas.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘You are doing your job’: Detained Rahul Gandhi offers water to police - watch
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi offered water bottles to police personnel while being detained during the opposition's protest in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi offered water bottles to police personnel while being detained during the opposition's protest in Delhi on Wednesday. Handing out the water bottles he was seen telling them, "You are all doing your work".Rahul was later released from Barakhamba Road police station, where he had been taken after police stopped opposition leaders from proceeding towards Jantar Mantar.Rahul Gandhi was among several opposition leaders and MPs detained as they attempted to reach the designated protest site to protest against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise. The leaders alleged that police stopped their buses and prevented them from moving towards Jantar Mantar.Priyanka Gandhi alleges MPs were manhandledThe confrontation saw several opposition leaders detained, including Congress general secretary Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, TMC Rajya Sabha MP Derek O’Brien and RJD MP Manoj Kumar Jha. Priyanka Gandhi alleged that police personnel manhandled MPs during the confrontation."This is how they treat Members of Parliament who are asking simply to meet the election commissioner. This is how they treat us. They are beating MPs. The Policemen have scratched me all over. They have thrown us to the ground. Now, we are not going to move from here. Let them crawl their forces back. I will not move from here."Priyanka Gandhi and other detained leaders were later taken to Chhatrasal Stadium. She said the opposition would continue to defend the Constitution."What is the value of the Constitution in this nation? We will lay down our lives for the Constitution.
